1. **me?** For centuries people called Mary something the Bible never called her, and it stuck. What label have I believed about myself that God never actually gave me?

**Am I staying, or am I among the ones who left?**

2. Nearly all the disciples fled. The women stayed at the cross, at real risk. Where is Jesus asking me to stay right now, in a place it would be easier and safer to leave?

**Is grief blinding me to what God is already doing?**

3. Mary stood feet from the risen Jesus and mistook Him for the gardener. What might God already be doing right in front of me that my sorrow has kept me from seeing?

## Today's Action

## Hear Your Name

Everything turned for Mary the moment Jesus said her name. Let Him say yours.

**1. Sit quietly and write down the false label you have been carrying as if it were your name.**

**2. Across it, write the name God actually calls you: His own, redeemed, sent. Read both out loud.**

**3. Then do what Mary did: tell one person your one true sentence, I have seen the Lord, what He has done in your life.**

One false label crossed out, one true name read aloud, one testimony spoken. Do it, and check it off.

## Today's Prayer

*Father,*

*You freed Mary Magdalene from a darkness that had a total hold on her, and then You trusted her with the first word of the resurrection. You redeem people the world writes off, and You hand them Your most important news.*

*I have worn false labels too, Lord. Things people decided about me, things I decided about myself, that You never once called me. Say my real name over all of it.*

**Call me by name, Lord, the way You called her. I want to know Your voice that well.**

*Make me one of the ones who stay. When it is dangerous, when everyone else is leaving, when there is nothing to gain and everything to lose, let me be found at the cross and at the tomb, still there.*

*And when grief narrows my whole world down to what I have lost, open my eyes to what You are already doing right in front of me. Help me keep looking through the tears until I see that You are the one standing there.*

*Thank You that relationship comes before assignment, that You spoke my name before You gave me a job. Having met You, send me like You sent her. Let my life say what she said first: I have seen the Lord.*

**In Jesus’ name, amen.**
reflection_question: What false reputation have I accepted as the truth about me?

day_title: Martha and Mary: Two Sisters, One Savior
devotional_text:
Two sisters loved Jesus with everything they had. They just did not love Him the same way. One ran to the kitchen the moment He walked through the door. The other sat down on the floor and listened.

Then their brother got sick. Then he died. And both sisters stood at that grave asking Jesus the exact same question: where were You when we needed You?

Maybe you already know which sister you are. Maybe you are the one who cooks, plans, and serves, and quietly wonders if anyone notices how tired you are. Or maybe you are the one who would rather sit still and listen, and you feel guilty for not doing more.

Both sisters wrestled, without ever saying it out loud, with the same fear: is the way I love God the wrong way?

On this last day of our study, we meet two women who answer that question together, and a Savior who loved them both, exactly as they were.

**Today we close with the sisters of Bethany, and the Jesus who wept before He worked a miracle.**

## Before You Read

In Luke 10, watch how Jesus corrects Martha. He says her name twice, and He never says serving is wrong.

In John 11, notice that Jesus deliberately waits two days after hearing Lazarus is sick, and that Scripture says He loved them in the same breath.

Watch both sisters say the identical sentence to Jesus, and watch Him answer each one differently.

## As You Read, Notice

What Jesus says is the one thing needful

Why Jesus waits before going to Lazarus

What Martha confesses about who Jesus is

What Jesus does at the tomb before He raises Lazarus

And think about this question: **is the way I love God the wrong way?**

“Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me... shall never die. Believest thou this?” (John 11:25–26)

## One Sister Serves, One Sister

## Sits

Martha and Mary were sisters in the village of Bethany, about two miles from Jerusalem, and they had a brother named Lazarus. Jesus loved this family and stayed in their home more than once. The first time we meet them, Jesus arrives, and Martha opens her home to Him, no small act of work and hospitality for a traveling teacher and His followers. And while Martha works, Mary does something unusual.

*“And she had a sister called Mary, which also sat at Jesus’ feet, and heard his word.” (Luke 10:39)*

Sitting at a rabbi's feet as a student was, in that culture, almost always reserved for men. Mary sat there anyway, and Jesus let her stay. Meanwhile the work piled up on Martha until she broke.

*“Lord, dost thou not care that my sister hath left me to serve alone? bid her therefore that she help me.” (Luke 10:40)*

Hear what she actually says. Not just, tell her to help. *Dost thou not care.* That is the sound of a tired heart, not just tired hands. Martha was not lazy or petty. She was exhausted and felt alone in it, and she said so out loud to Jesus, who did not scold her for saying it. His answer was tender and honest at once.

*“Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part.” (Luke 10:41–42)*

Saying her name twice is tenderness, not anger. And notice what He does not say. He never calls her serving wrong. He says she is *careful and troubled*, anxious and pulled in every direction, when only one thing was needed in that moment. Busy hands and a distant heart can happen even while doing good, useful things. This was never a contest between a good sister and a bad one. It was a loving correction about where Martha's heart had drifted while her hands stayed busy.

## A Brother Dies, and Jesus

## Waits

Some time later, Lazarus fell gravely ill, and the sisters sent for Jesus with a message full of confidence: *Lord, behold, he whom thou lovest is sick*. And then Scripture tells you something crucial right before the hardest part.

*“Now Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus. When he had heard therefore that he was sick, he abode two days still in the same place where he was.” (John 11:5–6)*

Read those two verses together, because they are meant to be read together. He loved them, **and** He stayed put anyway. Two more days passed while Lazarus worsened and died. This is one of the hardest truths in the Gospels: Jesus' love for this family did not mean an instant rescue. His delay was not neglect. It was aimed at something they could not yet see. If you have ever wondered why God lets suffering run its course instead of stopping it right away, this family lived that question before you did.

By the time Jesus arrived, Lazarus had been in the grave four days. Many believed a person's spirit lingered near the body three days; by the fourth, all hope was gone. And the sisters respond true to character. Martha, the one who moves, went out to meet Jesus on the road. Mary, the one who sits, stayed in the house. And Martha said one of the most honest sentences in the Bible.

*“Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died. But I know, that even now, whatsoever thou wilt ask of God, God will give it thee.” (John 11:21–22)*

That is grief and faith in a single breath. A little blame, spoken straight to His face, and then, without pausing, I still know God will give You whatever You ask. Jesus told her, *thy brother shall rise again*, and Martha answered with correct theology and a broken heart: I know he will rise at the last day. And Jesus lifted her eyes from someday to right now.

*“I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live... Believest thou this?” (John 11:25–26)*

And Martha, the woman we usually remember only for being *cumbered about much serving*, gave one of the clearest confessions of faith in the entire Bible: *Yea, Lord: I believe that thou art the Christ, the Son of God.* She said it before Lazarus walked out of the grave. She believed first, and saw second. Do not reduce Martha to the kitchen. In the worst week of her life, she spoke a creed the whole church still stands on.

## Jesus Wept

Then Jesus called for Mary, and she came and fell at His feet, the same place we first found her, and said the identical words her sister had said: *Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died.* Same grief, same ache, said on her knees. And Jesus did not answer Mary with a theology lesson. He answered her with His whole heart.

*“Jesus wept.” (John 11:35)*

The shortest verse in the Bible, and one of the most staggering. Jesus already knew He was about to raise Lazarus. He wept anyway. God in the flesh, standing feet from a miracle He was about to perform, still let Himself cry over the grief of people He loved. Why weep if you know the ending is good? Because sorrow is real even when hope is real. He did not need to grieve for information. He grieved because He loved them, and death is an enemy even to the God who is about to defeat it. Whatever these twenty one women have shown you about being seen by God, this verse shows you the heart behind the seeing. He does not watch your grief from a distance. He stands in it and cries.

Then He walked to the tomb and told them to take away the stone. Martha, ever practical, protested that after four days there would be a stench. Jesus reminded her: did I not tell you that if you believe, you would see the glory of God? They rolled the stone back, He prayed aloud for the crowd's sake, and then He cried with a loud voice, *Lazarus, come forth*. And a man four days dead walked out of his own grave, bound in his grave clothes. The One who wept at that tomb was the same One who had the power to empty it. Grief and power were never opposites in Jesus. They stood side by side at the same grave.

## The Perfume and the Close

There is one more scene, days before the Passover, back in Bethany. They made Jesus a supper, and *Martha served*. Still Martha. Still serving. And now nobody is arguing about it, because her serving, offered to Jesus with her heart in the right place, was always a beautiful thing. She had not changed who she was; she had learned where to put her heart while she worked. And then Mary did something extravagant.

*“Then took Mary a pound of ointment of spikenard, very costly, and anointed the feet of Jesus, and wiped his feet with her hair.” (John 12:3)*

A pound of pure spikenard was worth nearly a year's wages, perhaps her whole savings, poured out on His feet and wiped with her hair, something a respectable woman simply did not do in public. Judas objected that it should have been sold for the poor, but the text exposes him: he said it not because he cared for the poor, but because he was a thief. And Jesus defended her Himself: *let her alone: against the day of my burying hath she kept this*. Of everyone in that room, quiet Mary may have been the only one who understood what was coming. He had told the disciples plainly that He would die, and they kept missing it. The sister who listened at His feet was the one who was ready. Sometimes the person who loves quietly is paying closer attention than the ones doing all the talking.

Here is where this final day lands on you, and where our whole study comes to rest. There is more than one right way to love Jesus. Martha served and Mary sat, and He loved them both; you do not have to choose between them, only to know which one the moment in front of you calls for. Honest grief and real faith can live in the same sentence, the way they did in both sisters at that grave. Jesus grieves with you even when He is about to fix the thing, and delayed is not the same as denied. And what you pour out for Him, even when the world calls it a waste, is never wasted on Him.

For twenty one days you have walked from a garden to an empty tomb, meeting women God never once overlooked. Two of them, these sisters, loved Him in opposite ways and were both held close. That is where the study ends, and where your own story with Him begins. But today is not finished yet. Take the reflection questions first, then today's action, and end your day in prayer.

## Reflection Questions

Take a few minutes and answer these honestly.

**Which sister am I, and have I been judging the other one?**

1. Martha served; Mary sat; Jesus loved both and never ranked them against each other. Which am I by nature, and have I quietly looked down on people who love God the other way?

**Can I hold grief and faith in the same breath?**

2. Both sisters said if thou hadst been here, and both still trusted Him. Martha confessed her creed through tears. What am I grieving that I could bring to God honestly, without letting go of my faith to do it?

**What have I been afraid to pour out as a waste?**

3. Mary’s perfume was worth a year’s wages. Judas called it waste. Jesus called it beautiful. What costly thing is God asking me to pour out on Him that others might not understand?

## Today's Action

## Pour It Out

Mary poured out her most costly thing on Jesus, and He called it beautiful. Close this study with an offering.

**1. Name the one thing you have held back from Jesus because it felt too costly, your time, your plans, a resource, a dream.**

**2. Pour out a real portion of it on Him this week, deliberately, the way Mary broke the jar.**

**3. Then look back over these 21 days and write one sentence: what is the one thing you most need to carry forward from the women you met.**

One costly thing named, one real offering poured out, one sentence carried forward. Do it, and check it off.

## Today's Prayer

*Lord Jesus,*

**You loved Martha and Mary both, Lord. You let a woman serve and a woman sit and never once made them compete for Your love. Thank You that there is room at Your feet for who I actually am.**

*Forgive me for judging the people who love You differently than I do. Make me a Martha whose heart is where her hands are, and a Mary who is ready because she listened. Teach me which one each moment needs.*

*Thank You that I can bring You my grief and my faith in the same breath, the way both sisters did at that grave. I do not have to choose between being honest and being faithful.*

*Thank You most of all that You wept. That You, knowing the ending was good, still stood in their sorrow and cried. You do not watch my grief from far away. You stand in it with me, and You are never only grief, because You hold the power to empty the tomb too.*

*Help me pour out my costly things on You without counting the cost, the way Mary broke the jar. What I give You is never wasted.*

*And thank You for these twenty one days and these twenty two women. You saw every one of them, from the mother of all living to the sisters of Bethany, and You see me the same way. Let that be the thing I carry out of this book and into the rest of my life.*

**Amen.**

## Before You Close This Book

You made it. Twenty one days. Twenty two women.

You started in a garden with the first woman who ever lived. You stood outside an empty tomb with Mary Magdalene, the first person who ever saw the risen Jesus. And you finished in a home in Bethany, with two sisters who loved Him two different ways. From the first woman to the women at the empty tomb, the ones carrying this story were women. That is not an accident, and by now I hope you can see it.

Think back over who you just met. A mother who lost two sons in one day and trusted God for another. A slave girl who gave God a name. A wife nobody loved whose son carried the line of the Messiah. A widow who fought for her place. A harlot with a scarlet cord. A foreigner in a barley field. A mother who gave her only son back to God. A queen who said if I perish, I perish.

And yes, a queen who pulled a nation away from God, and a woman who sold out the strongest man alive for silver. The Bible kept them in the story too, because some lives are warnings, and a warning written down in love is still love.

Here is the thread that ran through all of it.

## People Overlooked These Women.

## God Never Did.

The LORD saw Leah. The LORD heard Hannah. God remembered Rachel. The God who sees found Hagar in the wilderness, twice. Jesus sat down at a well at noon for one woman the whole town avoided. And when He rose from the dead, He said one word, *Mary*, and sent a woman to carry the greatest news ever told.

So the next time somebody tells you the Bible has no place for women, you will know better. Women are not background characters in God's story. They are woven into every chapter of it, from the mother of all living to the mother of the Savior, and the family line of Jesus Himself runs through Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and the woman Matthew calls the wife of Uriah.

And the next time you feel overlooked yourself, unloved, unseen, stuck waiting on a promise that has not come, you now know twenty two women who stood exactly where you are standing. Go back and read their days again. That is why this book is built the way it is. It is not meant to be read once.

Keep reading your Bible. Every one of these stories is still sitting there in Scripture, with more detail than any study can hold. You know how to walk through a chapter now. Read it slowly, watch what God does, and ask what it means for your life today.

And if you want to keep studying with me, come join us on Bible Buddy at **www.mybiblebuddy.net**. It's free, and there are more studies like this one waiting for you.

Thank you for taking these twenty one days with me. I mean that.

## The God Who Saw Them

## Sees You Too.
reflection_question: Which sister am I, and have I been judging the other one?

day_title: Meeting God
devotional_text:
Every story has a first line. The first line of a story tells you what kind of story you are in. It tells you who matters. It tells you where to look. Get the first line wrong, and you will misread everything that comes after it. The Bible has a first line too. Before kings and battles. Before Abraham, before Moses, before Jesus walks the roads of Galilee. Before any of it, there is one sentence that opens the whole book. And that sentence does not start with us. It does not start with a man, a nation, or a problem that needs fixing. It starts with a Person. That is where this book starts too. Over the next 21 days we are going to walk through the first eight chapters of the Bible. We will watch God make the world. We will meet the first man and the first woman. We will see how a world God called good fills up with violence, and how God answers with judgment and with mercy, all the way to Noah stepping off the ark. But before any of that, we have to meet the One the whole story is about. Maybe you have heard about Him your whole life. Maybe you are just now opening the Bible for the first time. Either way, this is where we begin. Not with what people have told us about God, but with what God says about Himself. Today we are reading Genesis 1:1–2.

Before we read a single verse, let’s talk about the book we are opening.

The name *Genesis* comes from a Greek word that means origin or beginning. That fits. This is the book of beginnings. The beginning of the world, the beginning of people, the beginning of sin, the beginning of God’s promises.

In Hebrew, the language Genesis was first written in, the book is named after its very first word: *Bereshit*. It means in the beginning. The book is named after the first thing it says.

Genesis is the first book of the Bible. It is also the first of five books that the Jewish people call the *Torah*: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy. Torah is often translated law, but the word really means instruction or teaching. It is not just a list of rules. It is God teaching His people who He is and who they are.

Think about the opening of a movie. The first few minutes show you the world, the characters, the problem and what is at stake. If you walk in halfway through, you are lost. You do not know why people are acting the way they are.

Genesis is the opening of the Bible. Everything later points back here. God as Creator. People made by Him. A good world. Disobedience. Death. Violence. Mercy. Judgment. Then the long story of God rescuing what was broken. If you understand the beginning, the rest of the Bible starts to make sense.

This book covers Genesis 1 through 8. Creation, the garden, the fall, Cain and Abel, and Noah and the flood. Genesis itself keeps going for 50 chapters, through Abraham and his family, and it ends with Joseph in Egypt. We will get there in the books that follow.

So who wrote Genesis?

Jewish and Christian tradition has always credited it to *Moses*. Genesis does not sign its own name, but Moses is the man God used to lead Israel out of Egypt, and the first five books of the Bible have long been called the books of Moses.

Here is something worth stopping on. Moses was not there at creation. Nobody was. He lived many generations after Adam and Noah. In one traditional way of counting the years in the Bible, creation is placed around 4000 BC and Moses around 1500 BC. That is about 2,500 years between the first day and the man who wrote it down. Other people count it differently, but either way, it was a long time before him.

So how did he know?

God inspired what Moses wrote. That is the short answer. Moses may also have had stories passed down by families and written records kept over generations. God working through those and God revealing things directly are not opposites. God can use both. The way I picture it, I believe God could have shown Moses things in his encounters with Him, on the mountain and afterward. The Bible does not give us the exact method. It gives us the result: God’s true account of the beginning.

Now picture who Moses was writing for.

Israel had just come out of Egypt. For centuries they had lived there, and for a long time they were slaves, worked hard under cruel masters. Then God brought them out with plagues and a sea that split in two. Now they are camped in the wilderness on the way to the land God promised. Thousands of families. Tents. Dust. Not enough water. Not sure where the next meal is coming from.

These people already knew about God. Their families carried the names of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. They had just watched God do miracles in front of their eyes. And yet over and over, they struggled to trust Him. They got hungry and wanted to go back. They got scared and doubted.

Knowing about God and trusting God are not the same thing.

Genesis gave them roots older than Egypt. It told them who their God really is, where the world came from, where their family came from, and how they fit into a story much bigger than slavery.

And honestly, many of us are not that different.

A lot of us grew up hearing about God. Maybe from a grandmother who prayed. Maybe from parents who took us to church. Maybe from Bible stories we heard as kids. That is a gift. Faith handed down from people who loved us is a good thing, not something to throw away.

But there comes a point where hearing about God is not enough. Where we need to open the book and see for ourselves who He says He is.

We have heard about God. Now we are going to read and understand for ourselves. This is where we begin.

## In the Beginning God

> “In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.” (Genesis 1:1)

Stop at the fourth word. **In the beginning God**.

Before anything else is mentioned, God is already there. Not Abraham. Not Moses. Not Adam. The first person in the Bible is God.

So the natural question is, where did He come from?

And the answer is, He did not come from anywhere. Everything in this verse has a beginning. The heaven has a beginning. The earth has a beginning. God does not. He is not one more thing that somebody made. He is the One who made everything else.

That is what Christians mean when we say God is *eternal*. He has no beginning and no end. He is also *self existent*, which means He does not depend on anyone or anything for His life. You and I need air and food and a heartbeat. God needs nothing.

Psalm 90 is a prayer the Bible connects to Moses, and it says it like this:

> “Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever thou hadst formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God.” (Psalm 90:2)

Everlasting to everlasting. No starting line. No finish line.

There are three more words Christians use to describe God. They sound big, but they are simple, and they will help you all through this study.

God knows everything. Nothing is hidden from Him and nothing surprises Him. The word for that is *omniscient*, which means all knowing. Psalm 147:5 says of God, **his understanding is infinite**.

God can do anything He wills to do. Nobody is stronger. The word for that is *omnipotent*, which means all powerful. Jeremiah prayed, **thou hast made the heaven and the earth by thy great power**, and then he said there is nothing too hard for God.

God is present everywhere. There is no place you can go where He is not. The word for that is *omnipresent*, which means present everywhere. David asked, **whither shall I flee from thy presence?** The answer is nowhere.

Genesis 1:1 does not explain all of that in one verse. But watch the story. A God who knows everything, can do anything, and is everywhere at once is exactly the kind of God who could say a world into being.

Now look at what He made: **the heaven and the earth**.

That is a way of saying everything. Above and below. The Hebrew word for heaven can mean the sky above us or the place where God dwells, depending on the verse. Here, heaven and earth together means the whole created world. Nothing exists that God did not make.

But notice something. The world is not finished at the end of verse 1. There is no green grass yet. No oceans full of fish. Verse 2 shows us what it looked like at the very start.

> “And the earth was without form, and void; and darkness was upon the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters.” (Genesis 1:2)

**without form, and void**. In Hebrew that is two rhyming words, *tohu* and *bohu*. The simplest way to say it is unformed and unfilled.

Unformed means it has not been shaped yet. There is no dry land, no sky set in place, no order. Unfilled means nothing is living there yet. No gardens. No animals. No cities. No people.

This does not mean nothing existed. Something is there. It just is not ready to be lived in yet. Think about a plot of land before anyone builds on it. The ground is real. But there is no house, no garden, no family. That is the earth in verse 2.

It also does not mean the world was evil or ruined. The verse does not say anything went wrong. It is simply the starting point, like clay on the table before the potter shapes it.

Then it says **darkness was upon the face of the deep**.

*Face* here means the surface, the top layer. And the *deep* means deep waters. So picture darkness lying over the top of deep water. This is not empty outer space. It is a dark, watery world with nothing living on it yet.

And then comes the most important line in verse 2: **And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters.**

The word moved carries the picture of hovering, like a bird hovering over its nest. God is not off somewhere else waiting to show up. He is right there over the waters. Close. Active. Ready.

That tells us something about God. He is not a Creator who makes a world and walks away from it. He is near what He makes.

Who is the Spirit of God? Christians understand this as the *Holy Spirit*. The Bible teaches that there is one God who exists as three persons: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Not three gods. Not one God with a few helpers. One God, three distinct persons. Christians call this the *Trinity*.

Genesis 1:2 does not lay all of that out. It is an early thread, and the rest of the Bible pulls on it. Listen to how the Gospel of John opens, using the very same words Genesis does:

> “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The same was in the beginning with God. All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made.” (John 1:1–3)

Who is the Word? A few verses later John tells us:

> “And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us,” (John 1:14)

That is Jesus. So when we read Genesis 1 as Christians, we see God the Father creating, the Spirit of God hovering over the waters, and the Word, the Son, through whom all things were made. One God, already there, already at work. We will see another thread of this later in the chapter, when God says **Let us make man**. We will save that for when we get there.

So here is where Day 1 leaves us. The world is dark, watery, unformed and unfilled. But God is not missing from it. He is there, and His Spirit is moving.

Over the next few days we will watch God bring order. He will shape what was unformed. He will fill what was empty. That does not mean every hard thing in our lives disappears the moment we pray. But it does tell us what kind of God we are dealing with. He is not scared of the dark, and He is never far from it.

Here is a small thing to keep straight. The days of creation and the days of this study are not the same. On Day 2 of our study, we will read the first three days of creation, starting with four words: Let there be light.
reflection_question: What have you heard about God from other people that you have never checked in the Bible for yourself?

day_title: God Brings Order
devotional_text:
Think about the last time you walked into a dark room. You do not know where anything is. You bump into the table. You stub your toe. You cannot tell what is in front of you or what is behind you. Nothing makes sense until somebody finds the switch. Then the light comes on, and suddenly the room has a shape. Here is the floor. There is the door. Now you can actually live in it. That is where we left the world yesterday. Dark. Watery. Unformed and unfilled. But not empty of God. His Spirit was moving over the face of the waters. Now God is about to speak. And when God speaks, things happen. He does not struggle. He does not fight anybody for control. He says a word, and the world starts to take shape: light, then sky, then land, seas and plants. But watch closely. God is not just making things. He is building a world that keeps on working long after the day is over. God does not make one time objects. He makes systems that keep giving life. Today we are reading Genesis 1:3–13.

## A World Built to Keep Going

> “And God said, Let there be light: and there was light.” (Genesis 1:3)

That is it. That is the whole thing.

God said it, and it was. There is no fight. No struggle. No rival god pushing back. He did not have to work at it or try a few times. He spoke, and light was there.

Remember yesterday? We said God is *omnipotent*, all powerful. Here is what that looks like in action. His word alone is enough. A psalm says it simply:

> “For he spake, and it was done; he commanded, and it stood fast.” (Psalm 33:9)

Now here is something strange. Go and look ahead. The sun, the moon and the stars are not made until the fourth day of creation. We will read that in our next study day. Light shows up first.

That order is not an accident. God made light before He made the sun, and He did it on purpose.

Now, we know today that the sun makes its own light, and the moon reflects the light of the sun back to us. Genesis does not argue with that. The sun really does shine. But Genesis is answering a bigger question than how the sun works. It is telling us who is behind it. The sun did not make itself, and it did not invent light. It shines because God gave it that job.

Think about why that matters. In the world Moses was writing to, people worshipped the sun. Egypt had sun gods. Many nations looked up and bowed down. But Genesis says God made light first. The sun is not the source of everything. God is. The sun gives light because God made it to. Light was His idea before the sun ever existed.

> “And God saw the light, that it was good: and God divided the light from the darkness.” (Genesis 1:4)

Here is the first time in the Bible we read that something is good. And it is the light.

The Hebrew word is *tov*. It means more than nice. It means fitting, useful, working the way it should. When God sees the light is good, He is not surprised that His experiment worked. He is saying this is right. This is what it was made to do. This is good for life.

Then God *divided* the light from the darkness. Divided means separated, put each in its place. He did not destroy the darkness. He gave it a place and a limit.

> “And God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night. And the evening and the morning were the first day.” (Genesis 1:5)

God names them. Day and Night. When you name something, you are saying you are in charge of it and you know what it is for.

And notice that night is not evil here. Later in the Bible, light and darkness will be used as pictures of good and evil. But in this scene, night is just night. A time God made, named and gave a place. Sleep, rest, the stars. Night belongs to God too.

Then comes the line that repeats all through this chapter: **the evening and the morning were the first day**. A rhythm. Evening, then morning. A day is done. God is working in order, one step at a time.

Think about how much of your life runs on that rhythm. You wake up, you work, the sun goes down, you rest. Every single person who has ever lived has lived inside the pattern God set up on the first day of creation. That is not an accident either. God built the clock before He made anyone to live by it.

Now the second day of creation.

> “And God said, Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters.” (Genesis 1:6)

*Firmament* is an old word. In Hebrew it is *raqia*, and it means an expanse, a wide open space spread out. Verse 8 tells us what God called it: **God called the firmament Heaven**. Here that means the sky. Not the place we go when we die. The sky over our heads.

The words **in the midst of the waters** mean in between the waters. Remember, verse 2 showed us a dark, watery world. Now God opens up space in the middle of it. Water below. Water above. And an open sky between them.

The easiest way to picture it is to look up on a rainy day. There is water down here in the rivers and seas, and there is water up there that falls as rain. The Bible is not giving us a science diagram of the atmosphere here. It is describing what God did in words anyone could understand: He made room.

Read verse 7 and you will see three words that keep showing up: **and it was so**. God says it, and it is so. Every time. Nothing God commands falls short of what He said.

One small thing you might notice. The second day is the one day in this chapter where the words **it was good** do not appear. Do not read too much into that. God did not dislike the sky. The third day says it twice.

Now the third day.

> “And God said, Let the waters under the heaven be gathered together unto one place, and let the dry land appear: and it was so.” (Genesis 1:9)

The waters are pulled together, and dry ground shows up. God names it again. The dry land He calls *Earth*, which here means the ground, the land you stand on. The gathered waters He calls *Seas*. And God saw that it was good.

Do you see what God has been doing? On the first day He separated light from dark. On the second, the waters above from the waters below. On the third, the sea from the dry land. Separate. Name. Give it a place. Set a boundary.

That is what order looks like. Boundaries are not God being controlling. A sea that stays where it belongs is the reason you can build a house on dry land. God is setting up a home where life can grow.

And then life shows up.

> “And the earth brought forth grass, and herb yielding seed after his kind, and the tree yielding fruit, whose seed was in itself, after his kind: and God saw that it was good.” (Genesis 1:12)

*Grass* here means green growing plants in general. *Herb* does not just mean basil or the spices in your kitchen. It means plants that make seed. And then fruit trees, **whose seed is in itself**.

The words **after his kind** mean each one makes more of its own type. Apple trees make apples, not oranges. Wheat makes wheat. It is not a science lesson about species. It is a picture of order that keeps going.

Now stop right here, because this is the heart of today.

God did not just make a tree. He made a tree with seed in it.

Think about an apple. You eat it. You get to the middle, and there are the seeds. Plant one of those seeds, and in time it grows into a tree. That tree makes apples. Those apples have seeds. Those seeds make more trees. Again and again and again.

There is an old saying that you can count the seeds in an apple, but you cannot count the apples in a seed. One seed holds a tree. That tree holds hundreds of apples. Those apples hold thousands of seeds. It keeps multiplying, and it all started with one word from God on the third day.

God did not make one meal. He made food that keeps on making food. He did not set up a world that would run out after one season. He built something that would keep giving, year after year, generation after generation, long after the third day was over.

That is a *system*. God is not just a maker of things. He is a builder of systems that keep producing life.

This is not a promise that everything you touch will multiply and make you rich. That is not what the verse is about. It is about the kind of God we are reading about. He thinks ahead. He builds for the long run. He sets things up so life can keep going, even when nobody is watching.

And think about who that food is for. Nobody is there to eat it yet. No animals, no people. God is preparing the table before anyone sits down. He is providing before the need even shows up.

> “And the evening and the morning were the third day.” (Genesis 1:13)

So look at where we are. The world was unformed. Now it has a shape. Light and dark. Sky and sea. Dry land, covered in green, full of seed.

But it is still mostly empty. The sky has no sun yet. The waters have no fish. The land has no animals. There is a pattern starting here: three days to make the spaces, and three days coming to fill them. We will watch that happen next.

For now, hold on to this. The God who spoke light into the dark is also the God who put seed inside the fruit. He was not only thinking about that day. He was thinking about every day after it.
reflection_question: God spoke, and light was there. Do you treat God’s word like it actually has power?

day_title: A World Filled with Life
devotional_text:
Picture a brand new house the day before anyone moves in. The walls are up. The roof is on. The lights work. The kitchen is stocked. Every room is ready. But it is quiet. Nobody is walking the halls. Nobody is cooking. Nobody is laughing in the living room. A house can be finished and still be empty. That is what the world looked like at the end of our last reading. God had brought order. Light and dark were separated. The sky was spread out between the waters. Dry land stood above the seas, covered in grass and trees full of seed. Everything was in place. But almost nothing was living there. The sky had no sun yet. The seas had no fish. No bird had ever flown. No animal had ever walked across that green ground. That is about to change. In the first three days of creation, God made the spaces. Now He fills them. God does not just build a house. He fills it with life. Today we are reading Genesis 1:14–25.

## Forming, Then Filling

Before we read today’s verses, look at the pattern God is following. Once you see it, you cannot unsee it.

On the first three days of creation, God formed the world. He made the spaces. On the next three days, He fills those spaces.

Remember verse 2? The earth was **without form, and void**. Unformed and unfilled. Days one through three took care of unformed. Days four through six take care of unfilled. The problem in verse 2 is being answered one day at a time.

This is not a rigid chart. It is a pattern Moses wrote into the story so we would notice it. And it says something about God. He prepares the place before He brings the people. He made the plants before anyone needed food. Now He makes the creatures, and the home is already waiting for them.

Now let’s read.

> “And God said, Let there be lights in the firmament of the heaven to divide the day from the night; and let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and years:” (Genesis 1:14)

Remember what we saw last time. Light was already there on the first day. Now God makes the lights that carry it. The light came first. The lights come fourth.

The words **lights in the firmament of the heaven** mean lights in the expanse of the sky. We talked about the firmament on Day 2 of our study. This is describing what we see when we look up. The sun, the moon and the stars, shining down from above.

* Day one, light and dark. Day four, the sun, moon and stars.
* Day two, the sky and the waters. Day five, the birds and the sea creatures.
* Day three, the dry land and plants. Day six, the land animals, and then people.

Look at the jobs God gives them. First, **to divide the day from the night**. Then, **for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and years**.

That is a calendar. The sun tells you when the day starts and ends. The moon goes through its phases every month. The year turns around again. For thousands of years, people planted their crops, planned their journeys and counted their lives by those lights.

The word *seasons* here means more than summer and winter. It also means set times, appointed times. Later in the Bible, Israel’s feasts were set by the moon and the calendar. God built time into the sky.

And signs does not mean horoscopes. God is not telling us to read our future in the stars. He made the lights to mark time, not to control our lives.

> “And God made two great lights; the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night: he made the stars also.” (Genesis 1:16)

The *greater light* is the sun. The *lesser light* is the moon. They are called great because of how they look from where we stand and the big jobs they have, not because the sun is the biggest star there is.

And the moon does not make its own light. It reflects the light of the sun. But from the ground, at night, it rules the sky.

Now look at the word *rule*. To rule the day. To rule the night. That does not mean the sun and moon are gods. It means God gave them a job, and they do it.

This mattered to Israel. Egypt, where they had just come from, worshipped the sun. Other nations bowed down to the moon and the stars. Later Moses warned Israel not to do the same:

> “And lest thou lift up thine eyes unto heaven, and when thou seest the sun, and the moon, and the stars, even all the host of heaven, shouldest be driven to worship them, and serve them,” (Deuteronomy 4:19)

Genesis takes the things the nations worshipped and puts them in their place. The sun is not God. The moon is not God. They are lamps God hung in the sky. They work for Him.

And then, almost like it is no big deal, the verse says **he made the stars also**.

Think about that. Look up on a clear night far away from the city. More stars than you could ever count. And the Bible covers all of them in five words. That is how big God is. What looks endless to us is a side note to Him. The Bible says **He telleth the number of the stars; he calleth them all by their names**.

> “And God set them in the firmament of the heaven to give light upon the earth,” (Genesis 1:17)

God *set* them there. He placed them on purpose. And then, **God saw that it was good**.

Now the fifth day of creation.

> “And God said, Let the waters bring forth abundantly the moving creature that hath life, and fowl that may fly above the earth in the open firmament of heaven.” (Genesis 1:20)

On day two, God made the sky and separated the waters. Now He fills them both.

*Abundantly* means in huge numbers. Not a few fish here and there. The waters are teeming. Swarming. Full of life. *Fowl* is the old word for birds, anything with wings that flies. The open sky that was empty is now full of wings.

> “And God created great whales, and every living creature that moveth, which the waters brought forth abundantly, after their kind, and every winged fowl after his kind: and God saw that it was good.” (Genesis 1:21)

*Great whales* is how the King James puts it. The Hebrew word is *tanninim*, which means great creatures of the sea. Picture whales, yes, but also every giant thing that lives in the deep. The biggest creatures in the water were not an accident. God made them.

Think about the biggest animal you have ever seen in a picture. A blue whale is longer than a bus. Some creatures live so deep in the ocean that people have barely ever seen them. Every one of them was in God’s plan on the fifth day. A psalm looks at the sea and says it like this:

> “O LORD, how manifold are thy works! in wisdom hast thou made them all: the earth is full of thy riches.” (Psalm 104:24)

*Manifold* means many, and many different kinds. That is exactly what Genesis 1 is showing us. Not one kind of fish. Not one kind of bird. A world packed with variety.

And notice again the words **after their kind**. We saw this with the plants. Each creature makes more of its own type. Fish make fish. Birds make birds.

Now comes something new.

> “And God blessed them, saying, Be fruitful, and multiply, and fill the waters in the seas, and let fowl multiply in the earth.” (Genesis 1:22)

This is the first blessing in the Bible. God speaks over the creatures and says be fruitful and multiply. Have young. Fill the seas. Fill the earth.

What is a *blessing*? When God blesses something, He is not just wishing it well. He is speaking good over it and giving it the power to do what He made it to do. The fish do not multiply because they figured it out. They multiply because God blessed them to.

Do you remember the seed? On the third day of creation, God put seed inside the fruit so it could make more fruit, again and again. Now He does the same thing with living creatures. He does not make one generation of fish and stop. He blesses them to keep making more fish, for thousands of years.

This is the same God, building the same kind of world. A world that keeps going. A world that keeps filling. A system that keeps producing life long after the day it was made.

Now the sixth day begins.

> “And God said, Let the earth bring forth the living creature after his kind, cattle, and creeping thing, and beast of the earth after his kind: and it was so.” (Genesis 1:24)

On day three, God made the dry land and covered it in plants. Now the land gets its creatures. Genesis puts them in three groups.

*Cattle* in the King James does not only mean cows. It means livestock, the kind of animals people would later raise and keep. Cows, sheep, goats.

*Creeping thing* means the small creatures that crawl and move along the ground. Lizards, bugs, the little things you find under a rock.

*Beast of the earth* means the wild animals. Lions. Deer. Elephants. The ones that roam free.

Those are examples, not a full list. Genesis is not naming every animal. It is painting the picture of a land that is suddenly alive. Hooves on the ground. Something rustling in the grass. Something roaring in the distance.

And notice where they come from. **Let the earth bring forth**. The same ground that brought forth grass and trees on the third day now brings forth living creatures at God’s word. The land God prepared is now full of the life He planned for it.

> “And God made the beast of the earth after his kind, and cattle after their kind, and every thing that creepeth upon the earth after his kind: and God saw that it was good.” (Genesis 1:25)

Good again. Count how many times you have read that word in this chapter so far. God keeps looking at what He made and saying the same thing. This is right. This is working. This is how it should be.

Now step back and look at the world.

The lights are shining and keeping time. The seas are swarming. The sky is full of birds. The land is full of animals. And the plants God made are already there, ready to feed them all.

Think about how carefully this was done. The plants were made before the animals that eat them. The sky was made before the birds that fly in it. The seas were made before the fish that swim in them. Nothing showed up to a home that was not ready for it. God thought of everything before it was needed.

The house is not empty anymore.

But it is not finished either. The rooms are full, and still something is missing. God is about to make one more creature, and He is going to make this one differently than all the rest.
reflection_question: God made the sun and moon to serve Him, not to be worshipped. What things in your life have you looked to as if they were in charge?

day_title: Made in God’s Image
devotional_text:
Think about parents getting a nursery ready before a baby comes home. The crib is built. The clothes are folded. The diapers are stacked. There is a blanket on the chair and food in the cupboard. Nobody is sleeping in that room yet. But everything in it is waiting for one person. That is what the last few days have looked like. Light. Sky. Sea and dry land. Plants with seed inside them. Sun, moon and stars. Fish, birds, cattle and creeping things. Day after day, God has been getting the world ready. Ready for what? Ready for who? Today the answer arrives. On the sixth day God makes the one creature He has been preparing everything for. And He does it differently than anything else He has made. No Let the earth bring forth this time. Now God says Let us make man. Then He does something that should stop us in our tracks. He puts His own image on these people. He hands them the care of His world. And He sets food on the table before they are ever hungry. At the end of it all, God looks at everything He has made and says something He has not said once in this chapter so far. You were made on purpose, in the image of the God who made everything. Today we are reading Genesis 1:26–31.

## Made to Reflect Him

Look at how God speaks this time.

For five and a half days the pattern has been the same. God says **Let there be**, or **Let the earth bring forth**, or **Let the waters bring forth**. And it happens. The earth, the water and the sky all answer His word.

But now the words change.

> “And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth.” (Genesis 1:26)

God does not say let the earth bring forth man. He says **Let us make man**. It sounds like God pausing before His final work. Like a builder stepping back and saying, now for the most important part.

And did you catch the words us and our? Who is God talking with?

Go back to Day 1. In Genesis 1:2 we met **the Spirit of God** moving over the waters. And we read how John opens his Gospel: **In the beginning was the Word**, and **All things were made by him**. On Day 1 we said we would save **Let us make man** for when we got here. Now we are here.

The Word is Jesus. So when Christians read **Let us make man**, we read it right alongside those verses. One God. Father, Son and Holy Spirit. All there at creation, working together.

Two small words do not explain the whole teaching of the Trinity by themselves. But they fit right into it. The God who is making man has never been lonely. He has always lived in relationship. And He is about to make a creature who is built for relationship too.

So what does it mean to be made in God’s *image* and *likeness*?

An image is a reflection. Think about a mirror. Stand in front of one and your reflection moves when you move. It is not you. But it shows you.

That is the idea here. People are made to reflect God and to represent Him in His world. Not by looking like Him on the outside. The image is not about a face or a body. It is about what we are made to be and to do.

Think about what we have watched God do in this chapter. He creates. He thinks and plans. He speaks. He puts things in order. He calls things good. He cares for what He made. Now look at people:

No animal does all of that the way we do. That is the image of God showing through.

But be careful here. Reflecting God is not the same as being God. We do not get His unlimited knowledge. We cannot be everywhere at once. We do not have all power. And we did not make ourselves. He has always existed. We needed Him to give us life. A reflection always depends on the one it reflects.

Now look at verse 27. Moses says the same thing three times in one verse.

> “So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.” (Genesis 1:27)

Created. Created. Created. Like he wants it to sink all the way in. And look at the last line. **male and female created he them**. Both of them. The man and the woman carry the image of God. Not one more than the other.

* We create and build
* We reason and plan
* We love and live in relationship
* We know right from wrong, and we answer for it
* We work with purpose
* We care for what is put in our hands

This is where some readers get confused. Keep reading into Genesis 2 and you see God form the man first and then make the woman later. So when was she made?

Here is the key. Genesis 1 is the wide shot. It shows the whole week from far away. Genesis 2 slows down and zooms in on the personal details of the man, the garden and the woman. Same story. Different camera.

So the woman is not made thousands of years later. She is not made after God rests. She is right here in the sixth day. That is why verse 28 can say God blessed them and spoke to them. Both of them are there to hear it. We will watch the close up of her creation in a few days.

And notice which day this is. Not day five with the fish and birds. Day six, the same day as the cattle and creeping things. People are the last thing God makes.

Now back to verse 26. God says **let them have dominion**.

*Dominion* means rule. Authority. In plain words, God gives people the leading role over the animals. The fish, the birds, the cattle, the creeping things. Humans are put in charge.

But think about who is handing over that authority. God made all of it. It is His. So dominion is not ownership. It is management. A manager runs the store, but the store belongs to the owner. And one day the owner asks how it went.

That means authority comes with accountability. Dominion is never permission to be cruel, wasteful or careless with what God made. It is a responsibility to rule the way He rules. Wisely. With care. Helping things grow.

> “And God blessed them, and God said unto them, Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth, and subdue it: and have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over every living thing that moveth upon the earth.” (Genesis 1:28)

On Day 3 we watched God bless the fish and the birds, speaking good over them and giving them power to multiply. Now He blesses people, and He speaks to them directly. Life. Ability. Provision. Purpose. His favor resting on them.

Then He tells them what to do with it. Be fruitful and multiply. Have children and grandchildren and keep going. And *replenish* the earth. Replenish here simply means fill. It does not mean there was a race of people before them that disappeared and needed replacing. God filled an empty world with good things. Now He wants it filled with people.

And *subdue* it. Subdue means bring under control. Work the earth. Bring order to it. Make it produce. The same God who brought order to a dark and empty earth now tells people to keep that order going.

Notice the order again. Blessing first, then responsibility. God does not hand them a job and wait to see if they earn a blessing. He blesses them, then sends them out to work.

Now here is a question you might not think to ask. The people are alive. They have a job. What are they going to eat?

God already thought of that.

> “And God said, Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed, which is upon the face of all the earth, and every tree, in the which is the fruit of a tree yielding seed; to you it shall be for meat.” (Genesis 1:29)

Go back to the third day of creation, in verses 11 and 12. That is when God made the grass, the herbs yielding seed and the fruit trees. Three days before there was anyone to eat them. The food was ready before the people who needed it.

Remember from Day 2, an herb here means a plant that makes seed. And notice that both the plants and the trees carry seed. Eat the fruit, plant the seed, and more food grows. It is the same kind of system we saw on Day 2. God does not give one meal. He builds a supply that keeps going.

Then there is that word *meat*. **to you it shall be for meat**. Wait. Meat from plants?

In old English, meat just meant food. Any food. The Hebrew word here is a general word for food too. So when the KJV says **every green herb for meat**, it means green plants for food.

> “And to every beast of the earth, and to every fowl of the air, and to every thing that creepeth upon the earth, wherein there is life, I have given every green herb for meat: and it was so.” (Genesis 1:30)

Look at what that means. In the beginning God gave people plants and fruit to eat. And He gave the beasts and the birds green plants. No hunting. No killing for food. The world is at peace.

That changes later. After the flood, God tells Noah something new.

> “Every moving thing that liveth shall be meat for you; even as the green herb have I given you all things.” (Genesis 9:3)

Now animals are given as food too, along with the plants. The contrast is plain. In Genesis 1, plants. In Genesis 9, God adds animals. This is not a lesson about what you should eat for dinner. It is a picture of how different the world was before sin and death came in.

And then comes the last verse of the chapter.

> “And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. And the evening and the morning were the sixth day.” (Genesis 1:31)

Up to now God has looked at His work and called it good. Over and over. Good. Good. Good. Now for the first time He says **very good**.

And look at what He is looking at. Not just the people. **every thing that he had made**. The light, the sky, the seas, the plants, the animals, the food, the man and the woman. The whole thing, put together and working, is very good.

This is not God fixing failed experiments. Nothing earlier was bad. Every piece was good. But when the last piece is in place and the whole picture is finished, it is very good.

The evening and the morning were the sixth day. The work of creation is done.

So here is where Genesis 1 leaves you. You are not an accident in a corner of the universe. People were the last thing God made, made to reflect Him, trusted with His world, fed before they were hungry, and part of a finished creation that God Himself called very good. That is who you were made to be.
reflection_question: What changes when you see every person as someone made in God’s image?

day_title: God Rests
devotional_text:
Six days. Light. Sky. Sea and land. Sun, moon and stars. Fish and birds. Animals. And finally a man and a woman made in His image. At the end of the sixth day God looked at all of it and called it very good. So what does God do on day seven? He does not make a new planet. He does not make a new animal. He does not start a second project. He does not even look around for something to fix. He stops. That might sound like a small detail. It is not. Out of everything God could have done with that day, He chose to rest. And then He did something no other day had received. He blessed the day itself and made it holy. Thousands of years later, people are still living by that day. Whole families of churches gather on different days of the week because of it. And most of us still live like rest is something we earn only after everything is done. Which is never. So we keep going, tired, and call it normal. God rested, and He was not tired. Today we are reading Genesis 2:1–3.

## Finished, Not Tired

Three verses. That is all we have today. But these three verses close the whole first week of the world.

> “Thus the heavens and the earth were finished, and all the host of them.” (Genesis 2:1)

*Finished*. The Hebrew word means completed, brought to an end. Not abandoned halfway. Not dropped because God ran out of ideas. Done. Every part God planned to make is made.

And **all the host of them**. A *host* is a huge crowd, a whole array of things. Sometimes the Bible uses that word for an army, and sometimes for angels. Here it means everything that fills heaven and earth. The sun, moon and stars up above. The trees, the fish, the birds, the cattle and the creeping things down below. All of it. Complete.

> “And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made.” (Genesis 2:2)

God **ended his work**. This happens on the seventh day, but nothing new is created on that day. The seventh day is not another day of making. It is the day the making stops.

Then comes the big word. *Rested*. The Hebrew word here means to cease. To stop. It is closely tied to the word we know as sabbath.

So be careful how you picture this. God is not lying on a couch catching His breath. He is not sore from six days of work. Isaiah says it plainly:

> “Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary? there is no searching of his understanding.” (Isaiah 40:28)

God **fainteth not, neither is weary**. He does not get tired. So His rest is not recovery. It is completion. He had a plan. He carried it out. It was very good. Nothing was missing. So He stopped.

And stopping His creation work does not mean He stopped caring for the world. Jesus said **My Father worketh hitherto, and I work**. God still holds everything together. The sun still rises. Seeds still grow. What ended on day seven was the work of making the world, not the work of keeping it.

Here is something worth slowing down for. Rest is part of the good world. Sin has not come in yet. Nobody is worn out. Nobody is broken down. Rest is not a patch for a fallen world. It was built into the world from the start, back when everything was very good.

> “And God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it: because that in it he had rested from all his work which God created and made.” (Genesis 2:3)

God did two things to this day. He *blessed* it, and He *sanctified* it.

We have already seen God bless the fish, the birds, and the man and the woman. Blessing is God placing His favor on something and giving it purpose. But this time He blesses a day. Not a person. Not a place. A day. The blessing is not money or a gift box handed to the calendar. It is God marking that time as special.

*Sanctified* means set apart as holy. Separated out for God. And look at the reason given. **because that in it he had rested**. God set this day apart because He rested in it. That means time itself can be holy, not just people and places.

This is the first holy day in the Bible. It is not the last. Follow it forward.

Before Israel ever got the Ten Commandments, God was already teaching them the seventh day. In Exodus 16, God fed Israel in the wilderness with *manna*, bread that showed up on the ground every morning. On the sixth day He gave them twice as much, so nobody had to go out and gather on the seventh.

> “See, for that the LORD hath given you the sabbath, therefore he giveth you on the sixth day the bread of two days; abide ye every man in his place, let no man go out of his place on the seventh day.” (Exodus 16:29)

Then at Mount Sinai, God made it a command for Israel. And He pointed straight back to Genesis 2.

> “But the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God: in it thou shalt not do any work, thou, nor thy son, nor thy daughter, thy manservant, nor thy maidservant, nor thy cattle, nor thy stranger that is within thy gates: For in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that in them is, and rested the seventh day: wherefore the LORD blessed the sabbath day, and hallowed it.” (Exodus 20:10–11)

Look who gets rest. Not just the father of the house. The sons and daughters. The servants. The cattle. Even the stranger, the foreigner living in town. Nobody in that household was supposed to be worked into the ground.

And notice the verse right before it. **Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work**. The command is not only about stopping. It is about a rhythm. Work, then rest. Work, then rest. The same rhythm God showed in Genesis 1 and 2. Six days of making, then a day set apart.

That rhythm tells us something about both. Work matters, because God worked. Rest matters, because God rested. A life that is only work is out of step with how God built the world. And a life that never works is out of step too.

When Moses repeats the command in Deuteronomy, he adds another reason:

> “And remember that thou wast a servant in the land of Egypt, and that the LORD thy God brought thee out thence through a mighty hand and by a stretched out arm: therefore the LORD thy God commanded thee to keep the sabbath day.” (Deuteronomy 5:15)

Israel had been slaves in Egypt. Slaves never got a day off. Now God tells these former slaves, you rest, and you let the people who work for you rest too. Do not become Egypt to somebody else.

Then comes Jesus. The religious leaders of His day had stacked so many rules on the Sabbath that it felt like a weight. Jesus healed people on the Sabbath, and it made them angry. He answered them:

> “And he said unto them, The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath:” (Mark 2:27)

The Sabbath was a gift. It was made for people. And doing good, like healing someone who is sick, was never against holy rest.

Hebrews takes it one step deeper:

> “There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God. For he that is entered into his rest, he also hath ceased from his own works, as God did from his.” (Hebrews 4:9–10)

Rest is not only stopping your hands. It is trusting God enough to stop. Entering His rest means you stop trying to hold the whole world up by yourself.

Think about what that means for Israel in the wilderness. Every sixth day, they gathered double. Every seventh day, they stayed home and ate what God had already given. No new manna fell that day. They had to trust that yesterday’s bread was enough. That is what rest looked like. Trusting that God had already provided.

So if all of this started in Genesis 2, why do some Christians worship on Saturday and others on Sunday?

Start with the calendar. The Bible’s seventh day is Saturday. The Jewish Sabbath runs from Friday at sunset to Saturday at sunset, because in the Bible a day begins at evening. Remember **the evening and the morning** all through Genesis 1. Sunday is the first day of the week. A modern calendar that starts the week on Monday does not change that.

*Seventh Day Adventists* and some other Christians keep Saturday as their day of rest and worship. They believe the seventh day command still stands for believers today.

Most Christians gather on Sunday. Why? Because Jesus rose from the dead on the first day of the week.

> “The first day of the week cometh Mary Magdalene early, when it was yet dark, unto the sepulchre, and seeth the stone taken away from the sepulchre.” (John 20:1)

And the early believers met on that day:

> “And upon the first day of the week, when the disciples came together to break bread, Paul preached unto them, ready to depart on the morrow; and continued his speech until midnight.” (Acts 20:7)

About a hundred years after Paul, a Christian teacher named Justin Martyr described believers gathering every Sunday to read Scripture, pray and share the Lord’s Supper. He tied that day both to creation and to the resurrection. So Sunday worship did not start with the Roman emperor Constantine, as some people say. It was already happening long before him.

Even Sunday churches do not all see it the same way. Many Reformed churches call Sunday the Christian Sabbath. They believe the weekly day of rest moved to the Lord’s Day. The Catholic Church teaches that Sunday, the Lord’s Day, is different from the Sabbath, but that it fulfills what the Sabbath pointed to. Other Christians see the exact day as a matter of freedom, pointing to passages like Romans 14 and Colossians 2, while still gathering to worship every week.

> “One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind.” (Romans 14:5)

So the real question is not which day is number seven. Everybody can count. The real question is how the seventh day command applies to Christians after Jesus. Sincere believers land in different places on that. But every one of them can see what Genesis 2 shows us. God built rest into the world, and He set time apart as holy.

Now bring it home. God rested, and He was not tired. Most of us are tired, and we still will not rest.

Why? Because stopping feels like losing. If I stop, things fall apart. If I stop, I fall behind.

Some of us do not even know how to stop anymore. We rest with our phones in our hands and our minds still at work. Our bodies sit down, but nothing in us actually stops.

But rest says something. It says God is still holding the world when I put my work down. The sun came up this morning without any help from me.

And rest is not just doing nothing. Look at what filled the day in the Bible. Worship. Family. Mercy for the worker and even the animal. Rest has a shape, and it points back to God.

God finished His work, called it very good, and then He stopped. You will never finish all of yours. So the question is not whether you have earned your rest. It is whether you trust Him enough to take it.
reflection_question: When was the last time you truly stopped?

day_title: The Man and the Garden of Eden
devotional_text:
Have you ever watched a movie that opens with a wide shot of a whole city from the sky? You see the skyline, the rivers, the roads, the lights coming on. Then the camera drops down. It goes through one window, into one room, and stops on one person’s face. Now the story really starts. That is what happens in Genesis 2. If you read straight through, it can be confusing. The seventh day is finished. God rested. Then verse 7 says God formed man. Wait. Was man not already made on day six? Is this a second man? Did this happen on day eight? No. On Day 4 we called Genesis 1 the wide shot. Now the camera comes in close. Genesis 1 showed us the whole week. Genesis 2 goes back to the sixth day and slows it down. We get to watch God shape the man with His own hands. We watch Him breathe life into him, plant him a garden, and give him work, a command, and a need. The God of the whole universe gets personal. Today we are reading Genesis 2:4–18.

## The Camera Comes in Close

Look at how verse 4 begins.

> “These are the generations of the heavens and of the earth when they were created, in the day that the LORD God made the earth and the heavens,” (Genesis 2:4)

**These are the generations**. This is the first time Genesis uses these words. And it will not be the last. It is like a chapter title Moses built right into the story.

We hear the word generations and think of a family tree. Grandparents, parents, kids. But here it means an account. A history. The story of what came out of something. Watch it show up again and again:

Each time, the heading opens the story that grows out of that person or family. Terah’s heading is mostly about Abram. Isaac’s heading is mostly about his sons. So here, **the generations of the heavens and of the earth** opens the story of what happens inside the world God just made. And at the center of that story are people.

That is the real break in the story. Not the chapter number. Chapter numbers were added to the Bible much later to help us find our place. The storytelling shift is right here in verse 4.

And **in the day** here simply means when. When the LORD God made the earth and the heavens. It is not saying these things happened on the seventh day. It points back to the time of creation as a whole.

* Genesis 5:1, the book of the generations of Adam
* Genesis 6:9, the generations of Noah
* Genesis 11:27, the generations of Terah, which opens the story of his son Abram
* Genesis 25:19, the generations of Isaac

Did you notice the name changed too? In Genesis 1 it was God. Now it is *the LORD God*. When you see LORD in capital letters in the KJV, it stands for God’s personal name, Yahweh. Same Creator. But now that the story turns personal, so does His name.

Then verses 5 and 6 give us the background.

> “And every plant of the field before it was in the earth, and every herb of the field before it grew: for the LORD God had not caused it to rain upon the earth, and there was not a man to till the ground. But there went up a mist from the earth, and watered the whole face of the ground.” (Genesis 2:5–6)

The KJV sentence is a little hard to follow, so here it is plainly. Before the plants and herbs **of the field** were growing, God had not sent rain, and there was no man to work the ground.

*Till* means to work the soil. Plow it, plant it, cultivate it. A field is land somebody farms. So Moses is pointing at something missing. The ground is there, but nobody is working it.

This does not mean every plant from the third day vanished. A common way to read it is that Genesis 1 talks about plant life in general, and this verse talks about the growth of the field, the kind that needs rain and a farmer. One of the words can even mean wild shrubs. The earth did not go bare after creation. The farm is simply waiting for its farmer.

Instead of rain, **there went up a mist from the earth**. The Hebrew word is unusual, and some translations say a stream, or water welling up out of the ground. Either way the picture is the same. God was watering the surface of the ground from below. The *face of the ground* just means its surface.

Now the moment the whole passage has been leaning toward.

> “And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.” (Genesis 2:7)

*Formed*. This is the word for a potter shaping clay. Picture his hands on the wheel, pressing, smoothing, shaping the clay into exactly what he wants. That is how God made the man. Not from far away. Up close. On purpose.

And He made him from **the dust of the ground**. There is a wordplay in Hebrew that you cannot see in English. The word for man is adam. The word for ground is adamah. The man is named after the ground he came from. Later God will say **dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return**. We are made of humble stuff.

But dust does not walk. Dust does not think. A shaped body lying on the ground is still just a shape. Then God **breathed into his nostrils the breath of life**.

Think about how close you have to be to breathe into somebody’s nose. That is how personal God is with the first man.

And **man became a living soul**. A *living soul* here means a living being. A living person. The man is alive because God gave him life. Every breath you have taken today goes back to this one.

On Day 4 we saw the big picture. Man made in God’s image, given dominion over creation. Here is the other side. That same man is made from dirt and kept alive by God’s breath. Honored and humble at the same time. Made to reflect God, and completely dependent on Him.

## A Garden in Eden

> “And the LORD God planted a garden eastward in Eden; and there he put the man whom he had formed.” (Genesis 2:8)

Read it slowly. God planted a garden **eastward in Eden**. It does not say God planted Eden. The garden is inside Eden.

Eden is the bigger region. The garden is a special place within it. Think of a park in the middle of a city. The park is in the city, but it is not the whole city. People say Garden of Eden like the two words mean the same thing, but the Bible keeps them apart. Even the name Eden carries the idea of delight. A land of delight, and in it, a garden God planted Himself.

Then **there he put the man whom he had formed**. God did not form the man and leave him standing in an empty field. He prepared a home and set him in it.

> “And out of the ground made the LORD God to grow every tree that is pleasant to the sight, and good for food; the tree of life also in the midst of the garden, and the tree of knowledge of good and evil.” (Genesis 2:9)

Look at the two things said about these trees. They are **pleasant to the sight**, and they are **good for food**.

God did not only make the garden useful. He made it beautiful. He could have fed the man from plain gray trees. Instead He gave him a place worth looking at. Beauty matters to God.

Then two special trees are named.

*The tree of life* stands in the middle of the garden. Its name tells you its role. It is tied to life itself. In Genesis 3, God speaks of a man eating from it and living for ever. We will come back to that tree in a few days.

*The tree of knowledge of good and evil* is the other one. This does not mean God was against learning. The man was free to explore, to study, to grow wise. This tree is about something else. It is about deciding good and evil for yourself instead of trusting what God says is good. The tree itself is not evil. Everything God made was very good. The issue is the line God drew around it.

And one more thing. The Bible never says the fruit was an apple. It just says fruit. The apple comes from later art and tradition.

> “And a river went out of Eden to water the garden; and from thence it was parted, and became into four heads.” (Genesis 2:10)

One river flows out of Eden, waters the garden, and then splits into four *heads*, meaning four branches. Picture one source, then four rivers heading out across the land. Moses names all four, so let’s walk through them.

> “The name of the first is Pison: that is it which compasseth the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold; And the gold of that land is good: there is bdellium and the onyx stone.” (Genesis 2:11–12)

*Pison* winds around **the whole land of Havilah**. *Compasseth* means goes around. Havilah was a land known for its riches, and Moses lists them. The gold is good. There is *bdellium*, which most understand to be a sweet smelling resin from a tree. Translations have handled that word differently over the years. And there is the *onyx stone*, a precious stone, though exactly which stone is meant can vary. The point is clear. This is rich land.
