> “And the name of the second river is Gihon: the same is it that compasseth the whole land of Ethiopia.” (Genesis 2:13)

*Gihon* winds around the land the KJV calls Ethiopia. The Hebrew word is Cush. In other places in the Bible, Cush is the land south of Egypt. But here, near Eden, people disagree about which region is meant. So it is wise not to just draw this river through modern Ethiopia on a map.

> “And the name of the third river is Hiddekel: that is it which goeth toward the east of Assyria. And the fourth river is Euphrates.” (Genesis 2:14)

Now we hit names we know. *Hiddekel* is the Tigris River. The prophet Daniel later stood on its bank, and the Bible calls it Hiddekel there too. It flows by *Assyria*, a land in what is now northern Iraq. And the *Euphrates* keeps the same name we use today.

Here are all four together:

The Tigris and the Euphrates still flow today through the Middle East. But today they do not come from one shared river, and the Pison and the Gihon are not clearly known. So the two familiar names do not hand us a map to the garden. The world has changed a great deal since then, and the flood is still ahead in this story.

So why does Moses name them at all? Because he is telling his readers that Eden was a real place in the real world, near rivers they knew. This is not a fairy tale land. It is where human history started.

> “And the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it.” (Genesis 2:15)

God put the man in the garden **to dress it and to keep it**. *Dress* means work it, cultivate it. *Keep* means care for it, watch over it, guard it.

* Pison: around Havilah, the land of good gold, bdellium and onyx
* Gihon: around Cush, which the KJV calls Ethiopia
* Hiddekel: the Tigris, flowing toward the east of Assyria
* Euphrates: the river that still carries that name

Do not miss this. Work came before sin. The man had a job in paradise. Work is not the curse. The sweat, the thorns and the painful, frustrating toil come later as part of judgment. But work itself belongs to the good world. Remember the field in verse 5 with no man to till it? Now it has its farmer.

> “And the LORD God commanded the man, saying, Of every tree of the garden thou mayest freely eat: But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it: for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die.” (Genesis 2:16–17)

Look at the order. Before God gives one rule, He gives a huge yes. **Of every tree of the garden thou mayest freely eat**. Every tree. Freely. Only then does He name the one tree that is off limits.

One no, in a garden full of yes.

And the warning is serious. **thou shalt surely die**. Surely means certainly. This is not a small rule with a small cost. When we reach Genesis 3, the man will not drop dead the moment he eats. But death will begin its work in him, and his closeness with God will break. The rest of Genesis shows that warning coming true, one funeral at a time.

Why give a perfect man a command at all? Because love that cannot choose is not love. The tree gave the man a real way to trust God. Every day he walked past it and did not eat, he was saying, God, I believe that what You call good is good.

And then, for the first time in the whole Bible, God calls something not good.

> “And the LORD God said, It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him.” (Genesis 2:18)

Everything up to now has been good, and then very good. But **It is not good that the man should be alone**.

Think about what the man has. A body God shaped. Breath from God Himself. A beautiful garden. Food on every tree. A job. A clear command. And still something is missing. There is no one like him.

God says He will make him **an help meet for him**. Read that as a help, meet for him. *Meet* is an old word for suitable, fitting, matching. A helper who corresponds to him. Later people squeezed it into one word, helpmate, and made it sound like a lesser servant. But the Hebrew word for help here is the same word the Bible uses for God helping His people. **My help cometh from the LORD**. Nobody would call God a lesser servant.

So the place is ready. The food is ready. The work is ready. The command is given. But the man is still alone, and God Himself says that is not good. And God is about to do something about it.
reflection_question: God formed the man with His own hands and breathed life into him. How does that change the way you see your own life?

day_title: Adam, the Animals, and the First Marriage
devotional_text:
Imagine being the only person on earth. You live in the most beautiful garden that has ever existed. The trees are full of good food. A river runs through it. You have real work to do, and it is good work. And God Himself speaks to you. And still something is missing. All through Genesis 1, God looked at what He made and called it good, and at the end, very good. But at the end of our last reading, God looked at the man in the garden and said something new. For the first time in the Bible, something is not good. It is not good that the man should be alone. So what does God do about it? He does not tell Adam to be content and stop wanting more. He does not leave him to figure it out alone. He moves. First comes a long line of animals. Then a deep sleep. Then a woman, made by God’s own hands and brought to Adam like a gift. By the end of this reading we will see the first marriage in history. And we will see two people standing in the garden with nothing to hide. Hold on to that picture. We are going to need it very soon. Today we are reading Genesis 2:19–25.

## Bone of My Bones

Before we read one new verse, look back at the verse that closed our last day. Everything today grows out of it.

> “And the LORD God said, It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him.” (Genesis 2:18)

We met this phrase last time. A *help meet* is a helper who is fitting for him, a partner who matches him, the way a left hand corresponds to a right hand.

So God has said what He is going to do. Now watch what He does next. You might expect the very next verse to say, and God made the woman. It does not.

> “And out of the ground the LORD God formed every beast of the field, and every fowl of the air; and brought them unto Adam to see what he would call them: and whatsoever Adam called every living creature, that was the name thereof.” (Genesis 2:19)

Instead of the woman, God brings the animals. Every beast of the field. Every bird of the air. One after another, they come to Adam, and Adam names them.

Wait. Why would God do this right after saying Adam needs a companion?

Some people read this scene like God is trying things out. Like He is holding up a dog, then a horse, then a lion, to see if maybe one of them will work. That is not what is happening. God is not confused about what Adam needs. He already said it in verse 18. He knows exactly what He is going to make.

So why the animals? Look at how the story moves.

First, the naming is real. Adam really does it, and it really matters. On Day 4 we saw God give mankind *dominion*, the right and the responsibility to rule and care for His creatures. Here we watch that dominion begin.

In the ancient world, naming something showed authority over it. It also showed understanding. Adam is not picking random sounds. He is looking at each creature and saying what it is.

And God lets his word stand. **whatsoever Adam called every living creature, that was the name thereof.** Think about that. The God who named the day, the night and the seas in Genesis 1 now lets a man finish the naming. That is honor. God is treating Adam like a partner in His work.

Second, the naming shows something. Look at the end of the next verse.

> “And Adam gave names to all cattle, and to the fowl of the air, and to every beast of the field; but for Adam there was not found an help meet for him.” (Genesis 2:20)

There it is. *Cattle* here means the tame animals, the ones that live close to people. Then the birds. Then the wild animals. Adam names them all. And every single one of them is something he can name. Not one of them is someone who matches him.

Picture it. A lion walks by. Then a deer. Then an eagle. Back in Genesis 1, every creature was made **after his kind**. Every animal had others like it. And here stands Adam, made in the image of God, and there is nobody like him in the whole garden.

The naming does not create the problem. It puts it on display. By the time the last animal walks away, Adam can see for himself what God already said. He is alone.

Sometimes God lets us feel a need before He meets it. Not because He enjoys watching us want something. Because when the answer comes, we will know it is a gift and not something we built ourselves.

> “And the LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam, and he slept: and he took one of his ribs, and closed up the flesh instead thereof;” (Genesis 2:21)

> “And the rib, which the LORD God had taken from man, made he a woman, and brought her unto the man.” (Genesis 2:22)

Now God does the work, and Adam does nothing. He is asleep.

Adam did not design his wife. He did not help build her. He did not even watch it happen. Everything about this moment is God’s work from start to finish.

God takes one of his *ribs*, the curved bones along the side of your chest, and closes up the flesh where it was. Then from that rib, God makes a woman.

Notice where God took from. Not from Adam’s head. Not from his feet. From his side. Bible teachers have pointed to that for centuries. Not from his head to rule over him. Not from his feet to be walked on. From his side, to stand with him. That picture fits everything this chapter is saying. She is made to be beside him.

And look at the end of verse 22. God **brought her unto the man.** Do you see the pattern? God brought the animals to Adam. Now God brings the woman. The same God who walked every creature up to Adam now walks one more up to him. But this time it is different.

> “And Adam said, This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh: she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man.” (Genesis 2:23)

These are the first words from a human mouth that the Bible quotes. And listen to them. **This is now.** You can almost hear the relief. This one. At last. After all those creatures, this is the one.

**bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh.** Adam is saying, she is made of what I am made of. She is like me. She is my kind. Everything he could not find in the line of animals, he sees standing in front of him.

Then Adam names her too. He named every animal, and now he gives her a name: Woman. Why? **because she was taken out of Man.** In Hebrew the two words even sound alike. Man is ish. Woman is ishshah. The names themselves say these two belong together.

But notice the difference. When Adam named the animals, he named creatures that were different from him. When he names the woman, he names someone who came out of him. She is not one more name on the list. She is his match.

> “Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.” (Genesis 2:24)

Now the story stops and explains something. Verse 24 starts with **Therefore**. Because of what just happened, this is how it will be.

Wait. Adam had no father and mother to leave. So who is this verse for? It is for everyone who comes after. The writer is telling us that every marriage since then goes back to this moment in the garden.

Three things happen in this verse.

To *leave* means a new household begins. Your parents are still your parents, and you still honor them. But your first loyalty on earth shifts. A new family starts.

* Leave: a man leaves his father and his mother
* Cleave: he holds on tight to his wife
* One flesh: the two lives become one

To *cleave* is an old word that means to stick to, to hold on and not let go. Like glue. It is a word of loyalty and commitment. You do not cleave to someone for a season. You hold on.

*One flesh* means two lives are joined. Their bodies, their home, their future. The union is so close that God talks about it as if two people have become one.

Jesus Himself went back to this verse. When people asked Him about marriage and divorce, He did not start with the customs of His day. He went straight back to Genesis.

> “Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.” (Matthew 19:6)

*Twain* is an old word for two. *Asunder* means apart. Jesus is saying marriage was God’s idea, and God is the One who joins a husband and wife together.

That matters. Marriage was not invented by a king, a culture or a government. It started in the garden, with God bringing a woman to a man.

> “And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed.” (Genesis 2:25)

And here the first week of our study comes to a close.

Look at how far we have come. We met God before anything else existed. We watched Him bring order out of the dark. We saw Him fill the world with life. He made man and woman in His image. He rested. He planted a garden and put the man in it. And now He has given the man a wife.

And the last picture is this one. Two people, standing in the garden, with nothing on and nothing to hide.

*Naked* means without clothing. But this verse is about more than clothes. Look at the last words. **and were not ashamed.**

To be *ashamed* is to feel that hot rush in your face when you do not want to be seen. The urge to cover up, look away, hide. It is the feeling that says, if they really saw me, they would not want me.

Adam and his wife did not have that feeling. Not with each other. Not with God. There was nothing between them. No secrets. No fear. No hiding.

Hold that picture in your mind. Because in the very next chapter, these same two people will still be naked. Their bodies will not change at all. But something else will. Soon they will be sewing leaves together and hiding among the trees.

Something is about to change. And the first thing to break will be this beautiful line: naked, and not ashamed.
reflection_question: God saw Adam’s need before Adam said a word. What need in your life do you need to trust God with?

day_title: Temptation, the Fall, and Hiding from God
devotional_text:
Think back to the last picture we saw. A man and his wife, standing in a perfect garden. Nothing on. Nothing to hide. And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed. No fear. No secrets. No hiding from each other, and no hiding from God. Now hold that picture next to this one. The same man and the same woman, crouched down behind the trees. Leaves tied around their bodies. Hearts pounding. Hoping God will not find them. Same garden. Same two people. Same bodies. Something changed. What happened between those two pictures? How do you get from naked and not ashamed to hiding in the bushes? It did not take a war. It did not take years. It took one conversation, one choice and one bite of fruit. And here is the part that should make all of us lean in. The way it happened to them is the way it still happens to us. A voice. A question. Something that looks good. A choice. And then the hiding. This is where the second week of our study begins. Everything after this in Genesis, every murder, every flood, every broken family, grows out of what happens here. Today we are reading Genesis 3:1–13.

## Something Changed

> “Now the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which the LORD God had made. And he said unto the woman, Yea, hath God said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden?” (Genesis 3:1)

A new character walks into the story. The *serpent*. That is the Bible’s word for a snake. In Hebrew it is nachash.

Then the KJV says he was more *subtil* than any beast of the field. That is the old spelling of subtle. But here it does not mean quiet or hard to notice. It means crafty. Cunning. Clever in a sneaky way. The serpent is a skilled deceiver.

So who is this serpent? Genesis 3 does not stop to tell us. But the rest of the Bible does. In the last book of the Bible, John looks back and names him.

> “And the great dragon was cast out, that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world: he was cast out into the earth, and his angels were cast out with him.” (Revelation 12:9)

**that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan.** The *devil*, also called *Satan*, is God’s enemy. He is a fallen spiritual being who works against God and against God’s people. And here in the garden, he is speaking through a snake.

Now watch his method. This is how temptation works, then and now.

He does not walk up and say, come do something evil. He starts with a question. **Yea, hath God said.** In plain words: Did God really say that?

Look at what God actually said back in Genesis 2. **Of every tree of the garden thou mayest freely eat.** Every tree. Freely. Except one. That is a generous God. A whole garden full of good food, and one tree off limits.

Now look at how the serpent says it. **Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden?** He takes God’s generous yes and makes it sound like a stingy no. He makes the gift sound like a cage.

And notice where he moves her attention. Away from all the trees she can enjoy. Onto the one tree she cannot have.

Now hear this clearly. Asking questions about God is not wrong. We ask questions all through this study. That is how you learn. An honest question says, I want to understand what God said. The serpent’s question says, maybe God is not as good as you think. One draws you closer to God. The other pulls you away.

> “And the woman said unto the serpent, We may eat of the fruit of the trees of the garden:” (Genesis 3:2)

> “But of the fruit of the tree which is in the midst of the garden, God hath said, Ye shall not eat of it, neither shall ye touch it, lest ye die.” (Genesis 3:3)

The woman answers him. She knows there is a command, and she knows there is a warning. Death.

So now the serpent stops asking and starts contradicting.

> “And the serpent said unto the woman, Ye shall not surely die:” (Genesis 3:4)

> “For God doth know that in the day ye eat thereof, then your eyes shall be opened, and ye shall be as gods, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:5)

Wait. Read that again. God said **thou shalt surely die.** The serpent says **Ye shall not surely die.** He takes God’s exact words and puts a not in front of them.

Then he goes further. He tells her God is holding out on her. God knows that if you eat this, your eyes will open. You will be like Him. And He does not want that for you.

That is the real poison in this conversation. It is not just a lie about the fruit. It is a lie about God. The serpent wants her to believe God is not good. That God is keeping the best thing for Himself.

> “And when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasant to the eyes, and a tree to be desired to make one wise, she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat, and gave also unto her husband with her; and he did eat.” (Genesis 3:6)

Now she looks at the tree. And she sees three things.

Here is something easy to miss. Back in Genesis 2:9, God made every tree in the garden **pleasant to the sight, and good for food.** The trees were supposed to be beautiful. Good food and pretty fruit were God’s idea.

So the problem was not that the fruit looked good. Lots of things God made look good. The problem is that something looking good does not mean God said yes. This was the one tree God had said no to.

And remember, the Bible says fruit, not apple. The kind of fruit is not the point. The point is who it belonged to.

* It was good for food
* It was pleasant to the eyes
* It was desired to make one wise

So why is this a sin? It is not about a snack. God gave them a whole garden. This was the one thing He told them not to take. To eat it was to say, I believe the serpent over God. I want what God said no to. I want to be like God on my own terms. It was distrust, pride and disobedience all in one bite.

And look at the end of the verse. She **gave also unto her husband with her; and he did eat.**

With her. Adam is right there. He does not stop the conversation. He does not say, wait, that is not what God told me. He does not go and ask God. He takes the fruit and eats it.

Do not put all of this on the woman. God gave the command to Adam before she was even made. Paul later writes **Adam was not deceived.** In other words, Adam was not tricked the way she was. He chose. He is responsible for his own bite.

So both of them have eaten. Now, what about those wide open eyes the serpent promised?

> “And the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons.” (Genesis 3:7)

Their eyes were opened, just like the serpent said. But look at what they see. Not glory. Not greatness. Not power like God. They see that they are naked.

They were naked before this too. In Genesis 2:25 they were naked and not ashamed. Their bodies did not change. What changed was how it felt to be seen.

So they grab fig leaves and sew them together into *aprons*, simple coverings tied around the waist. The first thing human beings ever made after sin was a way to hide.

Think about that. Their first move was not to run to God and tell Him what happened. Their first move was to grab some leaves and try to fix it themselves.

> “And they heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden in the cool of the day: and Adam and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God amongst the trees of the garden.” (Genesis 3:8)

Now God comes into the garden. The word *voice* here can also mean the sound. They hear the LORD God coming. And this is not a far away God who cannot reach them. This is God coming close, into the place He made for them.

Before, that sound would have meant joy. Now it means fear. And where do they hide? **amongst the trees of the garden.** The same trees God gave them for food are now where they hide from Him.

> “And the LORD God called unto Adam, and said unto him, Where art thou?” (Genesis 3:9)

Wait. Does God really not know where Adam is?

Remember what we learned about God at the very beginning of this study. God is *omniscient*. That means He knows everything. God is also *omnipresent*. That means He is present everywhere. Adam cannot hide behind a tree from the God who made the tree.

So God is not asking because He lost track of Adam. He is asking so that Adam will answer. **Where art thou?** is an invitation. Come out. Stop hiding. Come and talk to Me. God could have dragged him out. Instead, He calls his name.

> “And he said, I heard thy voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; and I hid myself.” (Genesis 3:10)

Listen to Adam. **I was afraid, because I was naked; and I hid myself.** Put that right next to Genesis 2:25. Naked and not ashamed. Now naked and afraid. The fig leaves did not fix it. He is wearing them, and he is still hiding.

> “And he said, Who told thee that thou wast naked? Hast thou eaten of the tree, whereof I commanded thee that thou shouldest not eat?” (Genesis 3:11)

Now God asks two more questions. Who told you that you were naked? Did you eat from the tree I told you not to eat from? God is not asking for information. He is calling Adam to account. He is giving Adam the chance to say, yes, I did it.

> “And the man said, The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat.” (Genesis 3:12)

Look how Adam answers. **The woman whom thou gavest to be with me.** Just one chapter ago she was bone of his bones. Now she is the woman. And notice who else he points at. **whom thou gavest.** He is blaming her, and he is blaming God for giving her to him.

> “And the LORD God said unto the woman, What is this that thou hast done? And the woman said, The serpent beguiled me, and I did eat.” (Genesis 3:13)

Then God turns to the woman. And she points at the serpent. *Beguiled* means tricked or deceived. And she is right. She was deceived. But being tricked does not erase the choice. She still reached out and ate.

Notice how both of them end their answer. **and I did eat.** Both of them admit it. And both of them point at somebody else first.

So look at what one bite did. Openness turned into hiding. Love turned into blame. Walking with God turned into running from Him. That is the change, and it started with one question: did God really say that?
reflection_question: Where is a voice in your life asking, did God really say that?

day_title: Judgment and Leaving the Garden
devotional_text:
God has asked His questions. Where art thou? Who told thee that thou wast naked? What is this that thou hast done? And every answer came back with a finger pointing somewhere else. The man pointed at the woman, and at God for giving her to him. The woman pointed at the serpent. Now the serpent has nobody left to point at. So God speaks. This is the hardest part of the opening of Genesis to read. God speaks judgment over the serpent, the woman, the man and the ground itself. Pain comes into the story. Hard work and sweat come into the story. And death, the very thing God warned them about, becomes part of every human life from here on. Then the door to the garden closes behind them. But if you read slowly, you will see something else woven right through the judgment. A promise. A covering. A God who is still caring for the very people who just turned away from Him. Judgment is not the only thing God speaks in this chapter. Watch for the hope. Today we are reading Genesis 3:14–24.

## Covered and Sent Out

> “And the LORD God said unto the serpent, Because thou hast done this, thou art cursed above all cattle, and above every beast of the field; upon thy belly shalt thou go, and dust shalt thou eat all the days of thy life:” (Genesis 3:14)

God starts with the serpent. And notice something. He asked Adam questions. He asked the woman a question. He does not ask the serpent anything. He just pronounces judgment.

The word here is *cursed*. A curse in the Bible is not a magic spell or a bad word. When God curses something, He is declaring judgment on it, and the consequences come with His words.

**upon thy belly shalt thou go, and dust shalt thou eat.** Picture it. Crawling low on the ground. Living in the dust. In the Bible, licking the dust is a picture of being defeated and brought low. The one who tried to lift himself up by dragging people down is now pressed down to the dirt.

> “And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel.” (Genesis 3:15)

Slow down here. This is one of the most important verses in the whole Bible.

*Enmity* means hostility. Being enemies. God says there will be war between the serpent and the woman, and between their *seed*. Seed is an old word for offspring. Children. Descendants. So this war will not end with these two. It will run through history.

Then comes the battle itself. **it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel.** To *bruise* here means to strike or crush. Both sides get struck. The KJV uses the same word for both blows. But look where each blow lands.

The serpent strikes a heel. That hurts. It is real pain. But you can survive a wound to the heel. The woman’s seed strikes the serpent’s head. That is the deadly blow. That is the end of the snake.

Christians have long called this verse the first gospel. The *gospel* means the good news. Right here, in the middle of the first judgment, God announces that someone is coming from the woman who will crush the enemy.

And the New Testament tells us who. Jesus was born of a woman. On the cross the enemy struck Him, and He suffered and died. That was the heel. But He rose again, and through His death He broke the devil’s power. That was the head.

> “Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same; that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil;” (Hebrews 2:14)

John says it plainly too: **For this purpose the Son of God was manifested, that he might destroy the works of the devil.** And Paul tells believers **the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly.** Do you hear the echo of Genesis 3:15 in that word bruise?

So the very first time sin entered the world, God already had a plan to crush it. Before Adam and Eve took one step out of the garden, the promise was spoken.

> “Unto the woman he said, I will greatly multiply thy sorrow and thy conception; in sorrow thou shalt bring forth children; and thy desire shall be to thy husband, and he shall rule over thee.” (Genesis 3:16)

Now God turns to the woman. *Sorrow* here means pain. *Conception* is becoming pregnant. Remember, God told them back in Genesis 1 to be fruitful and multiply. That blessing is still there. Children will still come. But now bringing them into the world will come with real pain.

Then God speaks about her marriage. **thy desire shall be to thy husband, and he shall rule over thee.** Bible teachers read the desire part in more than one way. But the big picture is clear when you hold it next to chapter 2. There we saw a man and woman side by side, bone of his bones, one flesh, nothing between them. Now there will be strain and struggle in the closest human relationship on earth.

And hear this. God is describing what sin does to marriage. He is not saying a husband crushing his wife is His good plan. Genesis 2 shows us the plan. Genesis 3 shows us the damage.

> “And unto Adam he said, Because thou hast hearkened unto the voice of thy wife, and hast eaten of the tree, of which I commanded thee, saying, Thou shalt not eat of it: cursed is the ground for thy sake; in sorrow shalt thou eat of it all the days of thy life;” (Genesis 3:17)

Now God speaks to Adam. *Hearkened* means listened to and obeyed. Adam listened to his wife over the clear word God had given him. That is the charge.

A lot of us call these Adam’s curse and Eve’s curse, and that gets at the heart of it. But look closely at who God actually says is cursed. The serpent. And the ground. God curses the ground **for thy sake**, because of Adam. Adam and his wife carry the consequences.

> “Thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee; and thou shalt eat the herb of the field;” (Genesis 3:18)

> “In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.” (Genesis 3:19)

Here is something people often get wrong. Work is not the curse. Work was there before sin. Back in Genesis 2:15, God put the man in the garden **to dress it and to keep it.** Work was a good gift.

What changes is how work feels. The ground fights back now. *Thorns* and *thistles*, the prickly weeds that choke a field, will grow where he wants food. He will sweat for every meal. The work that was a joy becomes a struggle.

Do you see what sin did? It did not invent new parts of life. It damaged the good parts God already gave. Children were a blessing, now with pain. Marriage was a gift, now with struggle. Work was a joy, now with sweat.

And then the hardest line of all. **for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.** Go back to Genesis 2:7. God formed man **of the dust of the ground** and breathed life into him. Now God says the body will go back to the dust it came from.

God warned them: **in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die.** The serpent said they would not. The serpent was lying. Death has now entered the human story.

> “And Adam called his wife’s name Eve; because she was the mother of all living.” (Genesis 3:20)

Look at what Adam does right after hearing the word death. He gives his wife a name. *Eve*. In Hebrew the name sounds like the word for life. **because she was the mother of all living.**

Think about that. God just said they would die. And Adam names his wife Life. Every person who will ever live will come from her. In that name there is hope. Life will go on. And somewhere down that line will come the seed God just promised.

> “Unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them.” (Genesis 3:21)

Now go back to Genesis 3:7. Adam and his wife **sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons.** That was their answer to their shame. Leaves they picked and tied together with their own hands.

And it did not work. Adam was wearing those leaves when he said, I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself.

Now God makes them *coats of skins*. Real garments. And God Himself clothes them.

Stop and think about where skins come from. For there to be skins, an animal had to die. This is the first death we see in the Bible after the fall. And it happens so that Adam and Eve can be covered.

Their covering cost a life.

That is the picture Christians have seen here for a long time, and it runs all through the rest of the Bible. Later, God’s law will teach His people sacrifice, and the book of Hebrews sums it up: **without shedding of blood is no remission.** *Remission* means forgiveness, sins being sent away. And the New Testament tells us how God finally covers sin for good.

> “But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot:” (1 Peter 1:19)

Genesis 3:21 does not show us an altar or a sacrifice ceremony. It shows us God making clothes. But the picture is there. We try to cover ourselves, and our coverings fail. God provides a covering, and it comes at a cost. That points straight to the cross, where the cost was His own Son.

And notice what the clothing does not do. It does not cancel the judgment. They still leave the garden. The consequences still come. But they leave clothed by God. Judgment and care, side by side.

> “And the LORD God said, Behold, the man is become as one of us, to know good and evil: and now, lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever:” (Genesis 3:22)

**as one of us.** Who is us? Back in Genesis 1:26 God said, let us make man in our image. Christians hear in that us the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, one God speaking together.

Now they know good and evil. But not the way God knows it. God knows evil without ever doing it. They know it because they did it.

Remember the two trees in the middle of the garden. The tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and the *tree of life*. They ate from the wrong one. Now God keeps them from the other.

Why? Not because God is scared of them. Nothing a man does can threaten God. It is mercy. Picture living forever in this broken condition. Sin, pain, blame and shame, with no end, ever. God will not let that happen.

> “Therefore the LORD God sent him forth from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from whence he was taken.” (Genesis 3:23)

> “So he drove out the man; and he placed at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life.” (Genesis 3:24)

So God sends him out of the garden **to till the ground**. Same job as before. Harder ground.

Now here is a question worth asking. Where did they go? Remember from our day on the garden, the garden was planted **eastward in Eden.** The garden was inside a bigger region called Eden. So leaving the garden did not have to mean leaving all of Eden.

Verse 24 tells us where the guards stood: at the east of the garden. It tells us about the guards, not about Adam’s new address. Adam and Eve may well have stayed in the wider land of Eden for a time. Later, in Genesis 4:16, Cain goes out to the land of Nod, **on the east of Eden.** That is a different statement and a further step away.

And who stands guard? *Cherubims*. One is a *cherub*. Two or more are cherubim. The KJV adds an extra s. Forget the chubby baby angels on greeting cards. In the Bible, cherubim are powerful heavenly beings who guard and surround the presence of God. Later God will have golden cherubim made for the top of the ark of the covenant, where He met with His people.

Next to them is **a flaming sword which turned every way.** A blade of fire, turning in every direction. No way around it. The way back to the tree of life is shut.

That is how the garden story ends. A man and a woman, clothed in skins God made, walking out into a hard world, with fire behind them.

But do not forget what they carried out with them. A covering God gave. A name that means life. And a promise that one day the woman’s seed would crush the serpent’s head. The way to the tree of life was closed that day, but God had already promised the One who would open it again.
reflection_question: What does Genesis 3:15 tell you about how quickly God moves toward hope?

day_title: Cain and Abel
devotional_text:
Two brothers. Same mother. Same father. Same family story. They grew up hearing about a garden their parents could never go back to. They grew up working ground that fought back. They knew where the thorns came from. They knew why their parents wore clothes. Then one day, both brothers bring something to God. One gift is received. One is not. And before that day is over, one brother is lying dead in a field, and the other is telling God he has no idea where he is. How does that happen? How does a family go from one bite of forbidden fruit to a brother killing a brother in just one generation? That is the question we walk through today. And it is not a story about strangers. It is a story about what happens inside a heart when anger is left alone to grow. It is about a God who sees it coming and speaks up before it is too late. God warned Cain before he ever picked up his hand. That warning is the center of this whole chapter. Today we are reading Genesis 4:1–10.

## The Gift, the Warning, and the Field

The garden is behind them now. Adam and Eve are living east of Eden, working cursed ground, and their family is about to grow.

> “And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived, and bare Cain, and said, I have gotten a man from the LORD.” (Genesis 4:1)

When the Bible says Adam *knew* Eve, it means they came together as husband and wife. It is the Bible’s way of talking about sex inside marriage. And from that union comes the first baby ever born.

Think about that. Adam and Eve were never babies. Nobody had ever seen a child before. Eve holds her son and says, **I have gotten a man from the LORD.** She is giving God the credit. She is not saying the child is the LORD. She is saying, God helped me receive this son.

The name Cain sounds like the Hebrew word for getting or acquiring. So his name echoes what his mother said over him. I got a man, with God’s help.

> “And she again bare his brother Abel. And Abel was a keeper of sheep, but Cain was a tiller of the ground.” (Genesis 4:2)

Cain comes first. Then Abel, his little brother. And notice the words **she again bare**. That just tells us the next son we are going to follow. It is not a full list of every child in the house.

Later, Genesis 5:4 tells us Adam **begat sons and daughters.** So this family is bigger than two boys. The story simply zooms in on the two brothers this scene is about. Hold onto that. It is going to matter a lot when we get to Cain’s fear in the next part of the chapter.

Now look at their jobs. Abel is a *keeper of sheep*. That means a shepherd. He watches the flock, protects it, moves it to grass and water, and takes care of it. Cain is a *tiller of the ground*. That means a farmer. He works the soil and grows crops.

Both of those are good, honest work. Remember, Adam was put in the garden to work it and keep it. And after the fall God told Adam, **cursed is the ground for thy sake.** So Cain is doing the hard work his father was told would be hard. Farming is not a lesser job. Nothing in this story says God has a problem with farmers.

> “And in process of time it came to pass, that Cain brought of the fruit of the ground an offering unto the LORD. And Abel, he also brought of the firstlings of his flock and of the fat thereof.” (Genesis 4:3–4)

**In process of time** just means time went by. The boys are grown. They have their own work. And now they each bring an *offering* to God.

So is this the first sacrifice in the Bible? Back on Day 9 we saw God make coats of skins to cover Adam and Eve. Something died so they could be covered. But this is the first time we see people bringing something to God themselves.

The word for offering here means a gift. A present brought to someone to honor them. That is bigger than just an animal sacrifice. An offering says, God, everything I have came from You. I trust You. I honor You.

And let’s be clear about what an offering is not. It is not buying God’s approval. It is not feeding a hungry God. God does not need anything from us. The offering is about the heart of the one bringing it.

Now look closely at what each brother brings. Cain brought **of the fruit of the ground.** That is produce. Crops from his field. That is all the text says.

Abel brought **of the firstlings of his flock and of the fat thereof.** *Firstlings* means the firstborn. The very first lambs born in his flock. And the *fat* was seen as the richest, most valuable part of the animal. The best portion.

See the difference? Abel’s gift is described with care. First. Best. Cain’s gift is just described as produce. The Bible does not say Cain’s crops were rotten. It does not say he brought garbage. We are not going to make that up. But it also does not say he brought the first or the best. And the Bible tells us exactly that about his brother.

Giving God the first is a statement of trust. When Abel gives the firstborn, he is giving before he knows how the rest of the year will go. He is saying, God, You come first, and I trust You with the rest. That costs him something precious. It is not what he can easily spare.

> “And the LORD had respect unto Abel and to his offering: But unto Cain and to his offering he had not respect.” (Genesis 4:4–5)

Now this is a verse a lot of people read wrong. *Had respect* here does not mean Cain had no respect for God. It is talking about God. God looked with favor on Abel and his gift. God did not look with favor on Cain and his gift.

And look at the order. God had respect **unto Abel and to his offering.** The person comes first. Then the gift. Same with Cain. God is not only grading the gift. He is looking at the man bringing it.

So what was the real difference? The New Testament answers that for us.

> “By faith Abel offered unto God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain, by which he obtained witness that he was righteous, God testifying of his gifts: and by it he being dead yet speaketh.” (Hebrews 11:4)

By faith. That is the key. Abel believed God, and his gift came out of that faith. And 1 John 3:12 says Cain’s **own works were evil, and his brother’s righteous.** The difference was in the heart and in the life, and the gift showed it.

And just so nobody walks away thinking God hates vegetables. Later in Leviticus 2, God gives Israel a whole offering made of fine flour and oil. In the KJV it is called a *meat offering*, but as we saw on Day 4, meat back then simply meant food. It was a grain offering. God accepted it. So the problem was never that Cain grew crops.

Here is where it hits home for us. There is a big difference between giving God your best and just going through the motions. Two people can sit in the same church, sing the same songs and drop money in the same plate. One is saying, God, You come first. The other is just checking a box. From the outside they look the same. God sees the difference.

And it is not only about money. It is your time. Your attention. Your first thoughts in the morning. Does God get the first and the best, or whatever is left over at the end?

Now watch how Cain reacts. This is where the story turns.

The text says **Cain was very wroth, and his countenance fell.** *Wroth* means very angry. And when his *countenance* fell, his face fell. You could see it on him. Anger. Hurt. That dark look that comes over somebody’s face when they are stewing.

And God does not ignore it. God comes to Cain.

> “And the LORD said unto Cain, Why art thou wroth? and why is thy countenance fallen? If thou doest well, shalt thou not be accepted? and if thou doest not well, sin lieth at the door. And unto thee shall be his desire, and thou shalt rule over him.” (Genesis 4:6–7)

This warning is not filler between the offering and the murder. This is the center of the whole scene.

God asks Cain a question. Why are you angry? God already knows. He is giving Cain a chance to look at his own heart. Then God gives him a way forward. If you do well, will you not be accepted? The door is still open. Cain can still turn around.

Then God paints a picture. **Sin lieth at the door.** Picture a wild animal crouched outside your door, waiting. Low to the ground. Ready to pounce the moment you step out. That is what sin is doing to Cain. It wants him. **Unto thee shall be his desire.** Sin wants to take control of him.

But then God says, **thou shalt rule over him.** You can master this. You are not helpless. The anger is real, but the choice is still his.

That is so important. Anger is not a destiny. Being angry did not force Cain to kill anybody. But anger that is left alone, fed and protected, becomes resentment. Resentment becomes a plan. And a plan becomes an act. God stepped in at the very first step and said, stop here.

> “And Cain talked with Abel his brother: and it came to pass, when they were in the field, that Cain rose up against Abel his brother, and slew him.” (Genesis 4:8)

Cain did not listen. He talks with his brother. They go out to the field. And there, away from everyone, Cain rises up against Abel and kills him. *Slew* is just the old word for killed.

Notice how many times the text says **his brother.** Over and over. The Bible will not let us forget who this is. This is not an enemy. This is his own little brother.

Murder is a sin because every person is made in the image of God. We saw that back on Day 4. To kill a person is to destroy someone who carries God’s image, and to take a life that only God gave. Cain did not just hurt Abel. He struck at something God made and called very good.

> “And the LORD said unto Cain, Where is Abel thy brother? And he said, I know not: Am I my brother’s keeper?” (Genesis 4:9)

Does that question sound familiar? In the garden God asked Adam, **Where art thou?** And He asked Eve, **What is this that thou hast done?** God already knew the answers then. He knows now. He is not asking for information. He is calling Cain to own what he did.

And Cain lies straight to God’s face. **I know not.** Then he pushes back with a question of his own. **Am I my brother’s keeper?** A *keeper* is a guardian. Someone who watches over and takes care of another. Cain is saying, Is it my job to watch him?

Do you see the irony? Abel was a keeper of sheep. He spent his life watching over what was in his care. And Cain says, I am not my brother’s keeper. The man who just took his brother’s life now acts like his brother was never his concern.

Look at how fast this family went downhill. Adam blamed Eve. Eve blamed the serpent. Now Cain does not even bother to blame. He just denies.

> “And he said, What hast thou done? the voice of thy brother’s blood crieth unto me from the ground.” (Genesis 4:10)

**What hast thou done?** Almost the same words God said to Eve. And then this. The voice of your brother’s blood is crying out to Me from the ground.

Blood does not have a voice. But God is saying, this innocent life was taken, and the evidence is calling out for justice. Cain thought the field was private. He thought nobody saw. But God heard it all. You cannot hide a killing from the God who gave that life.

And look at the ground again. Man was formed from the dust of the ground. Then the ground was cursed because of sin. Cain spent his life working that ground. And now that same ground has received his brother’s blood. The ground keeps showing up in this story, and it is not finished yet.

Step back and see where we are. One chapter ago, it was a piece of forbidden fruit. Now it is jealousy, rejected correction and a brother lying dead in a field. Adam and Eve’s sin did not force Cain’s hand. Cain made his own choice. But sin is spreading, and it is spreading fast.

And still, before any of it happened, God came to Cain and said, you can rule over this. That same God is still speaking to angry hearts before the door opens.
reflection_question: Does God get your first and best, or what is left over?

day_title: Cain’s Judgment and the Land of Nod
devotional_text:
Cain’s brother is dead. His blood is in the ground. And God has just asked the question Cain cannot answer. What hast thou done? Now comes the sentence. Cain is a farmer. The ground is his whole life. It is how he eats. It is how he works. It is where he poured his sweat every single day. And the very ground he loved is about to turn on him. But listen to what Cain says when he hears his punishment. He is not crying about Abel. He is scared. Scared that somebody is going to find him and kill him. Wait. Who? If the only people on earth are Adam, Eve and Cain, who is Cain afraid of? That is one of the biggest questions people ask about Genesis. Where did Cain’s wife come from? Who were these people he was so afraid of? How did he end up building a city? Today we answer it plainly, straight from the text. The family was much bigger than four people. And Cain knew it. Today we are reading Genesis 4:11–18.

## Who Could Kill Cain?

Yesterday ended with blood crying out from the ground. Today God answers that cry.

> “And now art thou cursed from the earth, which hath opened her mouth to receive thy brother’s blood from thy hand; When thou tillest the ground, it shall not henceforth yield unto thee her strength; a fugitive and a vagabond shalt thou be in the earth.” (Genesis 4:11–12)

Look at that picture. The earth **hath opened her mouth to receive thy brother’s blood.** The ground does not have a mouth. But God is describing the soil swallowing the blood that Cain spilled. Cain poured his brother’s life into the dirt.

Now that same dirt will not work for him anymore. **It shall not henceforth yield unto thee her strength.** *Henceforth* means from now on. *Yield* means to give or produce. From now on, the ground will not give Cain its strength. He can plant all he wants. It will not come up for him the way it used to.

Do you see how personal this is? Cain is a farmer. The ground is his livelihood. It is how he feeds himself and his family. His violence did not just end his brother’s life. It wrecked his own life too.

Follow the ground through these first chapters. God formed man from the dust of the ground. Then the ground was cursed because of Adam’s sin. Cain became a tiller of that ground. Abel’s blood went into that ground. And now the ground refuses to serve the man who put it there. Sin does not stay in one place. It touches everything.

Then God says **a fugitive and a vagabond shalt thou be in the earth.** A *fugitive* is someone on the run. A *vagabond* is a wanderer, someone with no settled home. Put them together and you get a restless man who never stops moving. No roots. No rest. Always looking over his shoulder.

And just so we are clear, this is God’s sentence on Cain for murder. It is not saying that everyone today who is homeless or moving around is cursed. That would be reading something into the text that is not there.

> “And Cain said unto the LORD, My punishment is greater than I can bear.” (Genesis 4:13)

Listen to what Cain says. Not, I am so sorry. Not, I killed my brother. Not one word about Abel. Cain’s whole answer is about what is going to happen to Cain.

> “Behold, thou hast driven me out this day from the face of the earth; and from thy face shall I be hid; and I shall be a fugitive and a vagabond in the earth; and it shall come to pass, that every one that findeth me shall slay me.” (Genesis 4:14)

**Thou hast driven me out.** Does that sound familiar? Back on Day 9, God **drove out the man** from the garden. Now Cain is being driven out again. His parents lost the garden. Cain loses the settled life he had left.

And Cain says, **from thy face shall I be hid.** That does not mean Cain can actually escape from God. Nobody can. God is everywhere. It means Cain is losing his place near God’s presence. The closeness is gone.

Then comes the line that makes everybody stop. **Every one that findeth me shall slay me.**

Every one? Who is every one?

A lot of people read Genesis and picture only four people on the whole earth. Adam, Eve, Cain and Abel. And now that Abel is dead, there would only be three. So who is Cain scared of?

Here is the answer. Just because the Bible names four people does not mean those were the only four people alive. The Bible tells us the story it is focused on. It does not stop to list every baby born.

> “And the days of Adam after he had begotten Seth were eight hundred years: and he begat sons and daughters:” (Genesis 5:4)

Sons and daughters. Adam and Eve had many children. And they lived for hundreds of years. Genesis 5:3 tells us Adam was 130 years old when Seth was born, and the Bible ties Seth’s birth to the loss of Abel.

Now think about that. People often picture Cain and Abel as two young men right after creation. But Abel died before Seth was born, and Seth came when Adam was 130. So Cain and Abel could have been 29 and 27. They could have been 80 and 70. They could have been well over a hundred. Either way, these were not teenagers in an empty world.

And over many years, families multiply. Adam and Eve have sons and daughters. Those children grow up and have children of their own. Then those children have children. In just a few generations, one family becomes a crowd.

Picture a family with a hundred children. That is not a number the Bible gives us. It is just a picture of how big a family could get over that many years. Now picture one of those brothers, or a nephew, or a cousin, finding out what Cain did.

What is the first thing he is going to say? You killed somebody in our family.

That is what Cain is afraid of. Not strangers from some other race. His own relatives. Brothers. Nephews. Kinsmen who loved Abel and want payback. Cain knows exactly what he did. And he knows there are people out there who know it too.

> “And the LORD said unto him, Therefore whosoever slayeth Cain, vengeance shall be taken on him sevenfold. And the LORD set a mark upon Cain, lest any finding him should kill him.” (Genesis 4:15)

Now look at God. Cain just killed his brother. Cain lied to God’s face. Cain has not said sorry. And still, God protects him.

*Vengeance* is payback. Getting even. God says if anyone kills Cain, vengeance will be taken on that person *sevenfold*, which means seven times over. In the Bible, seven often carries the idea of something full and complete. God is saying, Do not touch him. I will handle this.

Why would God do that? Because God judges murder, but He does not hand the job of revenge to every angry relative. If everyone who was wronged went out and killed the one who wronged them, the killing would never stop. One death would lead to another, and another. God puts a stop to that cycle before it starts.

Then God **set a mark upon Cain.** A *mark* is a sign. Its job was protection. So that anyone who found Cain would not kill him.

People have guessed all kinds of things about that mark. A tattoo. A scar. A letter on his forehead. But the Bible points us to what the mark did, and that is what matters. It was God’s sign that said, this man is under My protection.

Think about the mercy in that. Cain took a life with no mercy. God answers with justice and mercy at the same time.

> “And Cain went out from the presence of the LORD, and dwelt in the land of Nod, on the east of Eden.” (Genesis 4:16)

*Nod* means wandering. So Cain, the man sentenced to wander, goes to live in the land of Wandering. The name of the place matches the sentence.

And notice where it is. **On the east of Eden.** Back on Day 9, God placed the cherubims **at the east of the garden of Eden.** That was the garden. This is Eden itself. Remember back on Day 6 we saw the garden was planted inside a bigger land called Eden. Cain is moving even further out. First the family was put out of the garden. Now Cain goes east of Eden. Further and further from where it all began.

The point of Nod is not a spot on a modern map. The point is the direction. Away.

> “And Cain knew his wife; and she conceived, and bare Enoch: and he builded a city, and called the name of the city, after the name of his son, Enoch.” (Genesis 4:17)

So where did Cain’s wife come from? She came from the same place everyone else did. The family of Adam and Eve. Remember, Adam had sons and daughters. Cain married one of the women from that growing family. There is no need to invent some other race of people out in the land. The Bible gives us one family, and everyone comes from it. She was part of that family, and she built a life with Cain east of Eden.

Then Cain **builded a city.** Do not picture skyscrapers and highways. A city back then would have been a settlement. A place with walls or shelters where people lived together. A home base.

And he names it Enoch, after his son. One quick note so we do not get mixed up later. This Enoch is Cain’s son. There is another Enoch coming in Genesis 5 from a completely different branch of the family, the one who **walked with God.** Same name, two different men.

Now here is what stands out to me. The way I read this, Cain is still trying to build his own security. God said he would be a fugitive and a vagabond. A wanderer. And what does Cain do? He settles down and builds a city. He puts his son’s name on it.

God never said, Cain, you are forbidden to build a city. But the man sentenced to wander is working hard to make sure he never has to. He is trying to make himself safe, make himself settled, make a name that lasts. His own way. On his own terms.

And that is not just Cain. That is us. When God says something hard over our lives, how often do we try to build our way around it instead of turning back to Him?

> “And unto Enoch was born Irad: and Irad begat Mehujael: and Mehujael begat Methusael: and Methusael begat Lamech.” (Genesis 4:18)

*Begat* means fathered. So Cain’s family line keeps going. Enoch, then Irad, then Mehujael, then Methusael, then a man named Lamech.

Cain’s line is growing. His city is standing. From the outside, it looks like Cain built himself a pretty good life east of Eden.

But a city built by a man running from God is still a man running from God. And the next man in his line is going to show us exactly where that road leads.
reflection_question: When you face the consequences of something you did, are you sorrier about what you did or about what it cost you?

day_title: Lamech and the Birth of Seth
devotional_text:
Picture a man standing in front of his two wives, chest out, voice loud. Listen to me, he says. A man hurt me, so I killed him. And if God promised to avenge Cain seven times, then I will be avenged seventy and seven times. That man is Lamech. He comes from Cain’s family line. And he is not hiding a killing in a field like his ancestor did. He is bragging about it. He turned it into a song. That is how far things have fallen in just a few generations. Cain lied about a murder. Lamech boasts about one. And right when it looks like the whole human family is sliding into darkness, the story turns. A baby is born to Adam and Eve. A son named Seth. And through Seth’s line, something begins that runs all the way through the Bible to Jesus. Two families. Two directions. One boasting in violence. One calling on the name of the LORD. God was not finished with this family. Not even close. Today we are reading Genesis 4:19–26.

## Two Lines, Two Directions

Yesterday we followed Cain’s family line. Cain had Enoch. Enoch had Irad. Irad had Mehujael. Mehujael had Methusael. And Methusael had Lamech.

So Lamech is about six generations down from Adam, through Cain. Now, there is another man named Lamech coming in Genesis 5. That Lamech is Noah’s father, and he comes from a completely different branch of the family. Same name, two different men. The Lamech we meet today is Cain’s Lamech.

> “And Lamech took unto him two wives: the name of the one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah.” (Genesis 4:19)

Two wives. This is the first time the Bible tells us about a man with more than one wife.

Go back to Day 7. When God made the first marriage, it was one man and one woman. **They shall be one flesh.** That was God’s design from the beginning. Now, a few generations later, Lamech takes two. The Bible does not stop to comment on it. It just shows us that God’s pattern is already being bent.

> “And Adah bare Jabal: he was the father of such as dwell in tents, and of such as have cattle. And his brother’s name was Jubal: he was the father of all such as handle the harp and organ.” (Genesis 4:20–21)

Now look at Lamech’s children. These are real talents.

Jabal is called **the father of such as dwell in tents, and of such as have cattle.** When the Bible says *father of* here, it does not mean he was everybody’s dad. It means he was the first. The founder. The pioneer. Jabal started a whole way of life, living in tents and moving with herds of livestock.

His brother Jubal was **the father of all such as handle the harp and organ.** He was the pioneer of music. The organ in the KJV is not a big church organ like we picture today. It was most likely a kind of pipe or flute. Jubal is the first musician the Bible names.

> “And Zillah, she also bare Tubal-cain, an instructer of every artificer in brass and iron: and the sister of Tubal-cain was Naamah.” (Genesis 4:22)

Then from Lamech’s second wife, Zillah, comes Tubalcain. He was **an instructer of every artificer in brass and iron.** An *artificer* is a craftsman. Someone who makes things with skill. Tubalcain was the one who taught people how to work with metal. Tools. Blades. Things made by fire and hammer.

And he had a sister named Naamah. The Bible gives us her name right alongside her brothers. In a list full of sons, a daughter is named.

So look at this family. Livestock. Music. Metalwork. That is a lot of human progress in one household. People are building, creating, inventing.

And none of that is evil. Raising cattle is not a sin. Playing music is not a sin. Working with metal is not a sin. God made people creative. These are good gifts.

But here is the lesson. Being talented is not the same as being faithful. A family can be full of skill and progress and still be walking away from God. Look at what their father says next.

> “And Lamech said unto his wives, Adah and Zillah, Hear my voice; ye wives of Lamech, hearken unto my speech: for I have slain a man to my wounding, and a young man to my hurt. If Cain shall be avenged sevenfold, truly Lamech seventy and sevenfold.” (Genesis 4:23–24)

Lamech says this like a poem. Like a song. And it is a song about killing.

**Hearken unto my speech.** *Hearken* means listen closely. Lamech wants his wives to hear this. **I have slain a man to my wounding, and a young man to my hurt.** In other words, a man wounded me, so I killed him. A young man hurt me, so I took him out.

Hebrew poetry often says the same thing twice in two different ways. So this could be one killing, described twice. Either way, the point is the same. Somebody hurt Lamech, and Lamech answered with death. Whether he is telling about something he already did or warning what he will do, he is proud of it.

Then he grabs the words God said about Cain. Remember yesterday? God said, **whosoever slayeth Cain, vengeance shall be taken on him sevenfold.** That was God’s protection. God was stopping a cycle of revenge killings before it started.

Lamech takes that and twists it. If Cain gets seven, I get seventy and seven. He takes God’s words of protection and turns them into his own brag about payback.

Do you see the escalation? Cain killed his brother and tried to hide it. Lamech kills a man over an injury and writes a song about it. Cain needed God to protect him from revenge. Lamech makes revenge his whole identity.

Why is that a sin? Because revenge takes the place of God. God said vengeance was His to handle. Lamech says, no, I will handle it, and I will handle it seventy times worse. That is pride. It is treating another person’s life as cheaper than your own pain.

And look how much the world has changed. In the garden it was a piece of fruit. Then a brother in a field. Now a man who brags about killing to his family. Sin is not just spreading anymore. It is being celebrated.

Now here is something beautiful. Thousands of years later, Peter asked Jesus how many times he should forgive his brother. Seven times? And Jesus said, **Until seventy times seven.** Lamech wanted seventy and seven of revenge. Jesus calls His people to forgiveness that does not run out. Lamech’s numbers, turned the other way around.

> “And Adam knew his wife again; and she bare a son, and called his name Seth: For God, said she, hath appointed me another seed instead of Abel, whom Cain slew.” (Genesis 4:25)

Right here, the story changes direction. We leave Cain’s line and go back to Adam and Eve.

Eve has a son and names him Seth. And she says God **hath appointed me another seed instead of Abel.** The name Seth sounds like the Hebrew word for appointed, or placed, or granted. Eve is saying, God has given me this son.

Listen to her words. **Instead of Abel, whom Cain slew.** Eve has not forgotten. She still carries the loss of one son and the crime of another. Seth does not erase Abel. A new child does not make grief disappear. But Eve sees this baby as God’s provision in the middle of her pain.

So when was Seth born? We have a clear anchor in the next chapter.

> “And Adam lived an hundred and thirty years, and begat a son in his own likeness, after his image; and called his name Seth:” (Genesis 5:3)

Adam was 130 years old when Seth was born. And Genesis 4:25 tells us Seth came after Abel was killed. Like we saw yesterday, that leaves plenty of years for many sons and daughters to be born in this family. Seth is not the third child Adam and Eve ever had. He is the son the story is about to follow.

And there is a reason the story follows him. This is why Seth matters to the whole Bible.

Remember Genesis 3:15? God promised that the seed of the woman would one day crush the serpent’s head. Now Eve calls Seth **another seed.** And it is through Seth’s family that the promise is carried forward.

Here are some of the big names in that line. Not every generation, just the milestones, with many generations in between:

Notice it goes through Judah. Not Joseph. Jacob had a famous son named Joseph, the one with the coat. But the line to Jesus runs through his brother Judah. And this Joseph is not the same man as Joseph the husband of Mary, who comes many centuries later.

Matthew 1:3 names Judah, Tamar and Perez in Jesus’ family line. In the KJV they are spelled Judas, Thamar and Phares. And Luke traces Jesus’ family all the way back, through Judah, Jacob, Isaac, Abraham and Noah, until it lands right here.

> “Which was the son of Enos, which was the son of Seth, which was the son of Adam, which was the son of God.” (Luke 3:38)

So this is not just another name in a list. Seth is a link in the chain that leads to Jesus. That does not mean everyone in Seth’s line was a good person. It means God was carrying His promise through this family, generation after generation.

And then the chapter ends with this.

> “And to Seth, to him also there was born a son; and he called his name Enos: then began men to call upon the name of the LORD.” (Genesis 4:26)

* Seth, son of Adam
* Noah, and his son Shem
* Abraham, then Isaac, then Jacob
* Judah, one of Jacob’s twelve sons, and Tamar, and their son Perez
* King David
* Jesus

Seth has a son named Enos. And then, **began men to call upon the name of the LORD.**

To *call upon the name of the LORD* means to pray to Him and worship Him. To cry out to God, to depend on Him, to name Him as your God out loud. Later Abraham builds altars and **called upon the name of the LORD.** It is the language of worship.

This does not mean nobody had ever worshipped God before. Cain and Abel already brought offerings. But something is starting here. People are gathering and calling on God together, as a family, as a people.

Look at the two endings side by side. Cain’s line ends this chapter with Lamech saying, Hear my voice. Listen to me. Look what I did. Seth’s line ends this chapter with people calling on the name of the LORD.

One man shouting his own name. A people calling on God’s name.

That is the choice in front of every one of us. Talent will not save you. Progress will not save you. Getting even will not save you. The ones who call on the name of the LORD are the ones walking in the line of the promise.
reflection_question: Is there someone who hurt you that you still want to pay back?

day_title: From Adam to Noah
devotional_text:
Have you ever skipped a list of names in the Bible? Most people do. You hit a page full of the word begat and huge numbers, and your eyes start sliding down looking for the next story. Genesis 5 is one of those pages. Ten men. Hundreds of years each. The same pattern of sentences over and over again. But slow down, because this list is doing something. Last time we read, Cain’s family was building cities and making tools, and his descendant Lamech bragged to his wives about killing a man. Then Adam and Eve had another son named Seth. And in Seth’s day, people began to call upon the name of the LORD. Genesis 5 follows Seth’s family. It carries the story all the way from Adam to Noah. And if you listen close, one short phrase keeps ringing like a bell at the end of almost every life. And he died. Then one man breaks the pattern. And at the very end of the list, a tired father names his baby boy with hope in his voice. Today we are reading Genesis 5:1–32.

## And He Died

Genesis 5 opens with a heading.

> “This is the book of the generations of Adam. In the day that God created man, in the likeness of God made he him;” (Genesis 5:1)

Remember the heading we noticed back in Genesis 2:4? **These are the generations of the heavens and of the earth**. Genesis uses lines like this as chapter markers. They say, here is the next part of the story, and here is the family it follows.

Now the book follows the family of Adam.

*Generations* here means the family record. The line of people who came after. And the word you will see all over this chapter is begat, which we met on Day 11. It means fathered. When it says Seth begat Enos, it means Seth became the father of Enos.

Before the list even starts, Genesis takes us back to the beginning:

> “Male and female created he them; and blessed them, and called their name Adam, in the day when they were created.” (Genesis 5:2)

Male and female. God made them both. God blessed them both. And He gave them both the name Adam, which means man, or mankind. The blessing from Genesis 1 still belongs to men and women together.

Then look at the very next verse:

> “And Adam lived an hundred and thirty years, and begat a son in his own likeness, after his image; and called his name Seth:” (Genesis 5:3)

Put those two lines side by side. God made man in the likeness of God. Now Adam fathers Seth in his own likeness, after his image.

Seth looks like his dad. That is part of it. But there is more going on. Adam is not passing down a life in the garden. He is passing down what he is now. A man made by God and still carrying God’s image. But also a man outside the garden. A man who is going to die.

God’s image did not get erased when Adam sinned. Later in Genesis, after the flood, God still says man is made in His image. The image is still there. But now it is being passed down by fallen people.

So every baby in this chapter is two things at once. A bearer of God’s image. And a child of Adam who will one day die.

Now let’s make the list easy to read. Every man gets the same three lines:

Take Adam. He was 130 when Seth was born. Then:

> “And the days of Adam after he had begotten Seth were eight hundred years: and he begat sons and daughters: And all the days that Adam lived were nine hundred and thirty years: and he died.” (Genesis 5:4–5)

130 plus 800 makes 930. Once you see that pattern, the whole chapter opens up. You do not have to decode every verse. Just follow the three lines. A son is born. Life goes on. Then the total.

And look at verse 4 again. **He begat sons and daughters**. Adam had a lot more children than Cain, Abel and Seth. That same phrase shows up for almost every man on this list.

* How old he was when a named son was born
* How many more years he lived, and that he had sons and daughters
* All his years added up, and then the words and he died

This is why Cain’s fear made sense back in Genesis 4. When he said someone might kill him, there were people out there. Brothers. Sisters. Nephews. Nieces. Their children. Years were passing and the family was spreading out across the land.

So this list is not everybody. It is one line. Genesis picks one son from each family and follows him all the way down to Noah. Here is that line:

Two of those names should sound familiar. There was an Enoch and a Lamech in Cain’s family too. These are different men. Same names, different branches of the family tree. And as we are about to see, very different lives.

Now the ages. Seth lived 912 years. Jared lived 962. Methuselah lived 969, the longest life recorded anywhere in the Bible. Genesis gives these years plainly, so we read them the way the story gives them. In the early world, people lived a very long time.

But here is the thing. A long life is not the same as no death.

Read the end of each life again. Adam, **and he died**. Seth, and he died. Enos, and he died. Cainan. Mahalaleel. Jared. Over and over and over.

* Adam
* Seth
* Enos
* Cainan
* Mahalaleel
* Jared
* Enoch
* Methuselah
* Lamech
* Noah

That phrase is the bell that keeps ringing through this chapter. You could live nine hundred years. You could watch your great great grandchildren grow up and have children of their own. And the bell still rings.

Go back to the garden. God told Adam that if he ate from the tree, **thou shalt surely die**. And after Adam ate, God said:

> “In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.” (Genesis 3:19)

Genesis 5 is that sentence coming true, one name at a time. The serpent told Eve, **Ye shall not surely die**. Genesis 5 answers him with a funeral at the end of every life.

Here is a detail that hits hard when you do the math. Add up the years, and Adam was still alive when Lamech, Noah’s father, was born. Adam lived 56 years into Lamech’s life. The man who once walked in Eden lived to see eight generations of his family. And then the bell rang for him too.

Then, right in the middle of all that death, something different happens.

> “And Enoch lived sixty and five years, and begat Methuselah: And Enoch walked with God after he begat Methuselah three hundred years, and begat sons and daughters:” (Genesis 5:21–22)

> “And all the days of Enoch were three hundred sixty and five years: And Enoch walked with God: and he was not; for God took him.” (Genesis 5:23–24)

Did you catch it? Every other life ends with and he died. Not Enoch. His ends with **he was not; for God took him**.

Enoch was not found anymore. He did not die like the others. God took him. The New Testament tells us what happened:

> “By faith Enoch was translated that he should not see death; and was not found, because God had translated him: for before his translation he had this testimony, that he pleased God.” (Hebrews 11:5)

*Translated* here means carried over. Moved from one place to another. God moved Enoch from this life to Himself without him passing through death.

And what does Genesis say about Enoch? Twice, it says he walked with God.

Walking with somebody is not a one time thing. You do not walk with a friend by taking one step next to them. You walk day after day, side by side, going the same direction. Enoch did that for three hundred years. Through raising children. Through a world that was getting worse around him. He kept walking with God.

Think about where this book started. In the garden, God came walking, and Adam and Eve hid from Him behind the trees. Now, outside the garden, here is a man who does not hide. He walks with God.

Hebrews says this was faith, and it tells us why it pleased God:

> “But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him.” (Hebrews 11:6)

What happened to Enoch was special. It was God’s choice for him, and Scripture does not hand it out as a promise to every believer. Faithful people still die. But every person who diligently seeks God finds out that He rewards them.

And look at this. Enoch lived the shortest life on the list, 365 years. His son Methuselah lived the longest, 969 years. But which life does the Bible hold up as the example? Not the long one. The faithful one.

Now look at the last full family on the list. Methuselah’s son Lamech has a baby boy. And for the first time in the whole chapter, a father tells us why he picked the name:

> “And he called his name Noah, saying, This same shall comfort us concerning our work and toil of our hands, because of the ground which the LORD hath cursed.” (Genesis 5:29)

Lamech is tired. Listen to him. Our work. The toil of our hands. The ground which the LORD hath cursed. He is talking about Genesis 3. The thorns and the thistles and the sweat. Generations later, people are still feeling it every single day.

The name *Noah* sounds like the Hebrew word for rest. And Lamech says **This same shall comfort us**. He is hoping this boy will bring relief.

Now compare the two Lamechs. Cain’s descendant Lamech stood in front of his wives and bragged about killing a man. He said if Cain is avenged sevenfold, **truly Lamech seventy and sevenfold**. Seth’s descendant Lamech holds his newborn son and speaks hope.

One Lamech talks about revenge. The other talks about rest. Two families. Same world. Same cursed ground. Very different hearts.

> “And Noah was five hundred years old: and Noah begat Shem, Ham, and Japheth.” (Genesis 5:32)

By the time Noah is 500, his three sons are in the story: Shem, Ham and Japheth. This does not mean they were triplets born on the same day. It tells us that from this point on, Noah is a father of three sons. Hold on to those three names. The whole world after the flood will come through them.

So no, this is not a page to skip. It is the story of a world where death keeps winning, one generation after another. And right in the middle of it, one man walks with God. And at the end of it, one father holds a baby and hopes for rest.
